From the Observer, August 28, 1853. CHOLERA AND CLEANLINESS. The return of the Registrar-General for the past week shows a slight decrease in the mortality from diarrhcca and cholera, as compared with the previous return. The deaths from the former disease amount to 126, and | burg, from the latter to 10. Diarrhoea has proved peculiarly fatal to infant life ; 97 children who died during the week had not completed their first year. This fact is of importance, as it at once puts an end to the popular fallacy that the increase of diarrhoea during the summer and autumn months is attributable to the consumption of fruit. The exciting cause may, in fact, be easily found in the increased temperature, and the consequent | direction than increased rapidity of decomposition. Vegetable and animal matter being, at this season of the year, more corruptible, noxious gases are thrown off during the process, and act as poison on the digestive organs. This being the case, how important is it that all refuse should be removed, before the hot season from our dwellings, and that works of purification should be actively pursued. The present return of the Registrar-General gives one or two cases which are shockingly corroborative of this. The registrar of one of the districts of Lambeth says, on recording the death of a child from diarrhoea þÿ This filthy hole (Isabella-place. Broadwall) is at all times rife with disease and death. My only surprise is that any human beings can exist in such an atmosphere ; yet every one of the seven or eight hovels it containsþÿ some

of two, others of four rooms þÿ has a family in each room. There is neither air, light, or ventilation of any kind. I do not register probably one-fifth of the fatal cases originating in this place, as many persons are removed to the workhouse or fever hospital, and are registered there. My return of this week is the largest in my sub-district since the period of cholera. Fever and diarrhoea are increasing." Several other instances arc

Similar observations have been made in the piovinces. From Hamburg there have been no further advices, and it is conjectured that the existence and spread of the disease in that city will be kept as long secret as possible, j The absurd quarantine regulations which are by many states strictly enforced against all ships coming from infected localities, renders the authorities anxious to keep the fact of the presence of the disease from being made public. The injury to the commerce of Hamshould it be considered an infected city, would be immense. We do not, therefore, anticipate receiving much information respecting the spread of the disease in Hamburg j until it has become so fatal that it cannot longer be hid. That it will become epidemic there we have no doubt. It has been attempted to be shown that because the disease has this year shown a tendency to proceed in a more northerly on former occasions, that, therefore, England is likely to escape. We

cannot see the force of this reasoning, for although the pestilence has proved exceedingly malignant and fatal whilst pursuing its northerly course, it has, nevertheless, steadily taken, at the same time a western route, and is now actually at the same western parts as in 1848. If, therefore, no steps have been taken either by the Government, the General Board of Health, the Commissioners of Sewers, the College of Physicians, or the boards of guardians, to meet the disease, should it become epidemic, unmitigated oensuie will most deservedly be cast on these several authorities should there be again a recurrence of the scenes of 1849, and the country be again found in a similar manner without preparation. The General Boaid of Health has no jurisdiction in the metropolis, and the responsibility of the health of 2,500,000 is, by a curious anomaly, confided to the Metropolitan Commission of Sewers. Under their several acts this body has extensive powers for the removal of nuisances, but so indifferent are they to the complaints of the public, or, perhaps, their hands are so tied up for money, thut up to the present moment we do not know of one single great nuisance having been removed through their agency. It is,

therefore, a question of immense importance that the public should take the matter into its own hands, and energetically call upon the authorities to protect them from sickness and death. It is all very well for the aristocracy and members of the Legislation, on the approach of a pestilence, to pack off to their country seats or watering places. The Overland Mail has brought intelligence of the loss of the ship Nessree on the coast of Hindostan, within 40 miles of Bombay, with upwards of 300 lives The particulars regarding the melancholy catastrophe, collected from papers that have since come to hand, areas follows: þÿ The Nessree was an English vessel, 500 tons burden, partly manned by a European crew, and for some years has been trading between Bombay and the various ports on the coast of Arabia. Early in April she was chartered to convey a number of pilgrims (who were returning, after a lengthened pilgi image through Arabia, to various parts of India) on a voyage to Bombay. She was lined up accordingly, and, on taking her departure, had. besides the crew, no fewer than 400 people on board, also a valuable cargo. The catastrophe happened on the night of the 7th of June. þÿI he evening previous the captain sighted Bombay, j but soon afterwards the weather set in thick, with rain and heavy squalls blowing on the land, amid which the ship got her rudder j unshipped, and. in consequence, became unmanageable. The passengers, ascertainin'; | the perilous position of the vessel, ami that | she was driving ashore, became frantic, and attempted to escape by the boats. The attempt, ns may be imagined, proved fatal. A | tremendous rush instantly capsized them, and at least (JO perished. The destruction of the j ill-fated vessel soon followed. Shortly after

niiiliiighi she struck, and the next moment her masts, with at least 100 of the unhappy creator dinging to the rigging, gave way and full overboard. The occupants were either crushed to death or peiished by drowning. In the course of a few hours the vessel entirely broke up, and the whole of the remainin': passengers and crew were plunged in among the breakers. Great sacrifice of life followed. Out of the 450 souls who were alive ilie, night previous, all, with the exception nf 04, perished. The 94 survivors were washed ashore on fragments of the wreck. What renders the catastrophe worse is, that no list or record exists from which could be gathered the names of the sufferers, or to what place in India tliev belonged. Amongst the many, who have been severe sufferers in the Danish Capital from the Cholera epideiny, which is raging there, the large number of children, who have been bereft of their parents, are without a doubt not least to be pitied. Although much has been done in Denmark, as well in a public way as through private charity, in order to relieve the immediate wants, still the misery is so great, and the means at hand proportionally so small, that every assistance will be welcome, and will find appropriate application. Trusting to the great benevolence, with which the inhabitants of the Danish West India Islands have ever been ready to succour their unfortunate fellow-creatures, without distinction of nations, the undersigned have joined, in order to appeal to those of our fellow-citizens, who are able and willing, to contribute their mite to the support of such children in the Capital, as liave lost their natural guardians from Cholera. Whatever may be tendered to us we shall be happy to receive, and shall transmit the amount collected as soon as possible to the Central Committee in Copenhagen. Should any-body wish their contribution applied to a more general purpose, than the one above stated, it is requested, that such an intention may be stated on sending us their gift. Regarding St. Croix Major Keutsch has kindly promised to receive any contributions, and remit the amount to us. St. Thorfias, 6tk September 1853. (Signed) A. STENERSEN. J. C. A. H1NGELBERG.

From the Dublin J Veekly Freeman's Journal, August 27, 1853. THE PLOUGH SUPERSEDED. TO THE EDITOR OP THE TIMES. Sir þÿ A calm and rigid investigation and computation have convinced me that the doom of the plough, as an instrument of culture, is sealed, and that the rotatory forking, or, as it. is wrongly called, digging machine, is the only profitable cultivator. Liven with six or eight horses, it is cheaper and infinitely more effective than the plough. Since the trial of implements at my þÿ gaþÿthering, I have received from one of our North American colonies the model of a newly-invented machine, which, by a happy \ and most simple combination of horse and I steam power, will þÿ and 1 pledge my agricultural reputation for it þÿ not only deeply, cheaply, and efficiently cultivate and pulverise the soil, but at the same time sow the seed and leave all in a finished condition. It will also, by a simple inversion, cut and gather the corn without any rake or other complication ; while both in cultivation and harvesting its operation will be continuous and without stoppage. The inventor and his machine have, by the government of the district, been placed under my charge and guidance. 1 have, therefore, on public grounds, and considering the vast importance of the invention in a national point of view, advised the inventor to grant licenses for its manulaeture at a very moderate royalty, to the most eminent agricultural implement-makers in various parts of the kingdom, so that our agriculturists may be secured by competition against monopoly or

inferiority, while the inventor will benefit in proportion to the appreciation of his merits. I shall call together a meeting of the various implement makers, and in due time my practical friends of the old school (who must now consider me quite insane) will have an opportunity on my farm of forming their own conclusions. 1 may venture to slate generally that the implement when complete will weigh about 20 to 25 cwt., will require a pair of horses, nnd will represent the power of about eight to twelve, or more, real horses.
a t

I trust I need hardly say that 1 shall have no pecuniary interest in this matter. The invention has been only secured. Your obedient servant, J J. MECHI. Tiptree-hall, Kelvedon, Essex. The implement for digging will require one man and one hoy only, including the management of the steam-engine ; in reaping, the same, with the addition of three men to bind as the corn falls into their arms. Sir Augustus Clifford, the Usher of the Black Rod, was then directed to summon the Commons, and immediately left the house. In a few minutes afterwards, the Speaker accompanied by the Sergeanl-at-Arms and Sir Augustus Clifford, and followed by Lord Palmerston, Mr. Brotherton, Sir G. Pechell, Lord D. Stuart, Mr. Walpole, and a considerable number of other members. The commission was then read by the clerk at the table, and the royal assent was given in the usual form to several public and private bills. The Lord Chancellor then read the royal speech, as follows; þÿ þÿ My Loros and Gentlemen: We arc commanded by her Majesty to release you from your attendance in Parliament, and at Ihe same time to express her þÿMajesty s cordial approbation of the zeal and assiduity with which, during a protracted and laborious session, you have applied yourselves to the

consideration of many subjects of great importance to the public welfare. þÿ Her Majesty has seen with much satisfaction that, by the remission and reduction of taxes which tended to cramp the operations of trade and industry, you have given Dcsh extension to a system of beneficent legislation, and have largely increased the means of obtaining the necessaries of life. þÿ The provision which you have made for meeting the demands of the public service, not only in the present but also in future years, is of a nature to give permanent stability to our finances, and thereby to aid in consolidating the strength and resources of the empire. þÿ The buoyant state of the revenue, and the steady progress of our foreign trade, are proofs of the wisdom of the commercial policy now firmly established ; while the prosperity which pervades the great trading and producing classes, happily without even a partial exception, affords continued and increasing evidence of the enlarged comforts of the people.

þÿ The measure which you have passed for the future government of India has been readily sanctioned by her Majesty, in the persuasion that it will prove to have been wisely framed, and that it is well calculated to promote the improvement and welfare of her Majesty's Eastern dominions. Her Majesty regards with peculiar satisfaction the provision you have made for the better administration of Charitable Trusts. The obstacles which existed to the just and beneficial use of property set apart for the purpose of charity and of education, have been a serious public evil, to which her Majesty is persuaded that in your wisdom you have now applied an efficient remedy. þÿ Gentlemen op the House of Commons : We are commanded by her Majesty to thank you for the supplies which you have granted for the service of the present year, and for the provision which you have made for the defence of the country both by sea and land. Her Majesty will apply them with a due regard to economy, and consistently with that spirit which has at all times made our national security the chief object of her care. þÿ My Lords and Gentlemen : Her Majesty commands us to inform you that she continues to receive from her Allies the as surance of their unabated desire to cultivate the most friendly relations with this country. þÿ It is with deep interest and concern that ncr Majesty has viewed the serious misunderstanding which has recently arisen between Russia and the Ottoman Porte. The Emperor of the French has united

with her Majesty in earnest endeavours to reconcile differences, the continuance of which might involve Europe in war. Acting in concert with her Allies, and relying on the exertions of the Conference now assembled at Vienna, her Majesty has good reason to hope that an honourable arrangement will speedily be accomplished. þÿ Her Majesty rejoices in being able to announce to you the termination of the war on the frontiers of the settlement of the Cape of Good Hope, and she trusts that the establishment of a Representative Government in that colony may lead to the development of its resources, and enable it to make efficient provision for its future defence. We are also commanded to congratulate you, that, by the united exertions of the naval and military forces of her Majesty and the East India Company, the war in Burmah has been brought to an honorable and successtul issue, the objects of the war having been fully obtained, and due submission made by the Burmese Government. Feace bas been pro claimed. þÿ Her Majesty contemplates, with grateful satisfaction and thankfulness to Almighty God, the tranquillity which prevails throughout her dominions together with that peaceful industry and obedience to the laws which ensure the welfare of all classes of her subjects. It is the first desire of her Majesty to promote the advance of every social improvement, and, with the aid of your wisdom, still further to extend the prosperity and happi- " ness of her people. MILITARY PROTECTION OF THE WEST INDIES. ( From the Port of Spain Gazette.) The mortality that has taken place among the Regiments stationed in the different West India Islands since the breaking out of the fearful epidemic which has now for a period of upwards of two years continued its lamentable ravages þÿ and still seems as far from relaxing its baneful influence as everþÿ cannot fail to claim the earnest attention of the military authorities, and should set them about devising some scheme to put a stop to, or, at any rate, lessen the fearful sacrifice of life at which the pro tection of a resident military force is afforded to the inhabitants of these colonies. But to withdraw the troops from the smaller and less important colonies, leaving only a few regiments located partly at Barbados, partly at Antigua, Trinidad, Demerara, and Jamaica, without making any arrangements provide to for the danger of insurrectionary movements among the lower classes of the inhabitants of the other colonies, is to cut fhe Gordian Knot þÿ not to undo it. The very serious disturbances which have just taken place at Tortola þÿ :he recent outbreak at Tobago þÿ lo say nothing of the riots of a not very far off date at Castries, Port of Spain þÿ more than suffice to shew that order cannot be maintained in any of the West India Colonies, without a resident military force of some description. Before intel licence can be sent off to the fortunate island at which troops arc stationed, and those troops can he conveyed to the scene of action, the most lamentable and

fearful results may ensue. Nay, we do not see bow such a course of proceeding can result otherwise than in the exodus from the colonies thus left without mill tary protection, of every respectable and intelligent inhabitant, whether of Euro pean, or mixed, or pure African descent, who has the slightest self-respect, oi love of order and tranquillity. That the lower classes of these colonies, thus left to themselves þÿ all the light of European civilization suddenly withdrawn þÿ would rapidly degenerate, in their mode of living and pursuits, to a par with those of their African progeni tors before these latter were brought to these colonies, can hardly be doubted, and although the sage politicians of the new school who have found out that the West Indies are only a burthen, and a costly incumbrance " to the Mother Coun- try, instead of the bright gems of the British Crown" they had been so long considered, would willingly throw them off, and leave them to shift tor themselves ; yet even they must pause and reflect over the consequence of leaving such populous localities as Tobago. Grenada, St. Vincent, St. Kitts, Domini-

ca, St. Lucia, Montserrat, Nevis, Tortola, Auguilla, and the Bahama Islands þÿ these latter standing in the very "high road" of commerce þÿ to become nests of pirates and barbarians, who would not be content with destroying the crews and passengers of every vessel wrecked on their shores, but would no doubt fit out small vessels in which to cany on their predatory excursions on a sea j which offers so many facilities to piratical enterprises. This þÿ at least, it no , higher and holier motive can influence the politicians of the present þÿday is a consideration that may well make them pause before they "shuffle off" the care and keep of the numerous islands thus proposed to be deprived of military pro- to tection, and left so unceremoniously the consequences that may ensue. The question then, that, it seems to us, ought to present itself to the minds of the military authorities in England, ;s þÿthis how military protection can still be afforded the inhabitants of the West Indies, but without the awful sacrifice of human life at which it is at present afforded; and without the immense expense attendant on recruiting the ranks of the regiments, to supply the vacancies occasioned by tropical diseases. As to any scheme of forming native companies þÿ -the ranks to he recruited from the labouring population of these colonies a little reflection þÿ will shew such a plan would never succeed. So long as the proprietary body ot these þÿislands the owners of the sugar estates and other properties of importance þÿ arc

principally "white," and the labouring population " þÿblack" so long as the principal authorities of the colonics are distinguished by complexion from those who till the soil þÿ so long party feelings of " black" and "white" must be liable to occur, and when they do occur, the men of these native companies, there is too much reason to tear, would he found taking the side of those of their own complexion, and becoming formidable partizans in a disturbance, instead of the quellers of it. Neither do the lower classes of these colonies þÿ native horn shew any predilection for the habit of discipline and self-abnegation which the military profession requires. As to the African regiments now in existence, they have on several occasions shewn their readiness to sympathize with their own colour (for which we are far from blaming them), and as the old, steady men die oft, the recruits in their stead Captured þÿ þÿAfricans are little to be depended upon, and exhibit great repugnance to the discipline to which they arc subjected. The days of these regiments are already looked upon by military men as fast drawing to a close. But there is another source from whence troops well fitted to stand the climate might be obtained, and who, being neither "white" nor "black," neither European nor African, would act « entirely under the command of their officers, in all cases, without sympathising with any local feelings or prejudices; and from this source England has alrea-

3 <6 IK it S A T it 3 dy, and with the same view ol avoiding a painful sacrifice of human life, drawn very largely in supplying the necessary amount of military force in another part of the British Dominions where the cli. mate is quite as obnoxious to European constitutions as is that of these colonies þÿ we allude to those natives ol the East Indies known as Seapoys, and from whom the ranks of the " Native Regiments" of India are recruited. These people have shewn themselves, under European officers, brave, excellent soldiers, all that could be desired for such services as those they would have to perform here. Their food is principally rice, and the cost of their maintenance in these colonies, as compared with tlr.it ; of European troops, would be but trifling. Regiments of these men might be gradually formed and drilled in India, the preference being given in the appoint- , ment of junior officers for such Regiments, to young men of good family, and good education, who had been born in West India Colonies, and who would not be so liable as Europeans to fatal results from tropical diseases. These Regiments might be then brought on here þÿ after which all vacancies in the appointment of officers could be filled up in the þÿColonies a military college being, if necessary, established at the Colonial Head Quarters þÿ þÿBarbados where the necessary military instruction could be imparted. Thus these Seapoys regiments might be gradually distributed throughout the different Island- . taking the place of the European regi-

ments, which might then be safely withdrawn, and sent on other services more congenial to the European constitution. We have thrown out these suggestions with the hope of their attracting attention in the proper quarter ; and should they hare the effect ol expediting the adoption of such measures as, whilst they will ensure the continuance of military protection to all ot the Colonies, yet will put a stop to the painful sacrifice of the lives ot as many gallant men who after daring and escaping the þÿ dangers of battle and siege, fall an inglorious prey to the diseases of a tropical þÿclimate great indeed will be our reward !

A short sermon, by a Quakeress, runs as follows: þÿ "Dear friend, fihere are three things 1 greatly wonder at. I lie first is, that children should be so toblish as to throw up stones, clubs, and brickbats, into fruit trees to knock down fruit; if they would let it alone, it would fall

THE MINISTER AND HIS SLAVE. The following is from the Neic York Tribune. The comments appended to the narrative it contains are so natural, and are so forcibly expressed, that we abstain from curtailing it. That its first appearance in England was in the columns of' the Times , is a significant circumstance : þÿ About fifteen years ago there came to Indianapolis, Indiana, a coloured man, named John Freeman. lie brought with him some few hundred dollars, a part of which lie interested in real estate. lie was a painter, whitewashes a man of all work. He married a young woman who was servant in a family here. His deportment won for him general respect and confidence, lie rapidly increased m property, and he is now worth about 15, (KM) dollars; which for that community is a very handsome property. No man's word was better than Freeman's. He was honest, punctual, and reliable. He became an active member of the coloured Baptist Church, and conscientiously discharged his duties as a church member. He has a family of three children. On the 23rd of June, a man named Pleasant Ellington, formerly from Kentucky, now of Missouri, who is, we understand, a Methodist preacher, appeared in Indianapolis, and found miscreants base enough to assist him in arresting Freeman, upon the claim that he was his slave. Freeman claims that he is a free man, and shows many papers recognising that fact. The judge has granted nine weeks for Freeman to procure further evidence of his freedom. There are some facts that have come

to our knowledge which it will be edifying to disseminate. When Freeman's arrest was known, the whole community was moved. One hundred men of all parties, and of the first standing in the þÿplace such as Judge Blackford, Judge YV'ickc, Air. N. B. Palmer, Mr. Calvin Fletcher, and many other such þÿ signed a bond for bail in the sum of I ,<>00 dollars. The amount, in gold, was brought into court, to be deposited for the preacher Ellington, in case Freeman, proved a slave, should not appear, or for his freedom in any event. The bail was refused. The Rev. Mr. Ellington refused to agree to take any price should he get possession of him, but determined to take him to Missouuri. Under a pretence that he feared a rescue, the marshal was about to re-

move Freeman to Madison gaol, on the Ohio river, but has consented to leave him in the gaol at Indianapolis, on condition that Freeman pays three dollars a day for a guard to watch over himself? We have some good but dull men in New York, who have denied that Christian men and families were subject to separation and sale under the system of slavery It is said that to represent such scenes as Uncle Tom's separation from his family and his wife is a slander. Yet, here is a preacher of the gospel making a pilgrimage of more than half a a thousand miles to find and arrest member of a Christian church, in a free State, and drag him into slavery. He finds him settled down in a home which his own industry had secured, with a wife and three children, a useful and greatly respected citi'/en One would think that a man with a particle of humanity, even if Freeman were his slave, upon seeing such a state of things would refuse to break up and desolate a family and blight the prospects of a fellow man and Christian. Hut sd deeply has this fellow drunk of the " spirit of patriotism" that he determines to make the mischief. Bonds and security were offered him the most ample, for any price that he might demand, in case Freeman should be proved his slave. He refused every thing. He demanded the man and declared that he would remove him to a slave state and to slavery. A man that can read such a state of facts, and not feel his heart rising with indignation against this scoundrel cler-

gyman, ought to regard himself as having sinned away his day of grace and as sealed over to reprobation. And yet, is this man any worse tjian the law allows? þÿ has he done anything illegal? This American people have laws by which men may violate every sentiment of humanity, smother every breath of Christianity, crush an innocent and helpless family, reduce a citizen of universal respect and proved integrity to the level of a brute, carry him to the shambles, sell him for ever away from his church, his children and his wife ; all this may be done without violating the laws of the land þÿ nay, by the laws and under the direction of magistrates. And so deadening has been the influence of slavery upon the public mind that religious teachers and religious editors will not find a single word to say against this utter abomination, and many pious words will they utter in favour of this execrable traffic. Meanwhile, that same God who permits the existence of tarantulas, scorpions, and other odious vermin, suffers also the existence of such creatures as this Rev. Mr. Ellington. It may serve a good purpose, in a glossing, timid, shuffling age, to exhibit it before the sun how utter a villain a man may be and yet keep within the pale of the law, within the permissions of the Church, and within the requirements of the Christian ministry. To crush the human heart, to eat up a living household, to make a family into one's hands and crush it like a cluster of grapes, tins is respec-

table, legal, and Christian, in the estimation of cotton patriots, and patriotic Christians, who regard law as greater than justice, the Union as more important than public virtue and practical Christianity. Such a law as that which permits these scenes will destroy the conscience and humanity of the community, or be itself destroyed by them. A people that have learned to see such sights unmoved are not far from the level of the Romans, whose amusements were in blood and death of beasts and of gladiators. þÿ St. Lucia Palladium.

Colonel P. de Nully, K. It. &c. &,c. &,c. Dear and valued Sir, Wc the undersigned, Officers of the Militia ol St. Croix, beg leave, on vour retirement from office as Stadshauptmand, after having honorably filled that situation for a lull quarter of a century, to oiler to you the expression of our heartfelt esteem and gratitude for the manner in which you have discharged your duties, as Chief of the Militia. It gives us a high degree of pleasure to notice our sense of the justice, urbanity, and kindness, which during the longer or shorter periods in which we have had the honor ot serving under you, we have invariably experienced at your hands, and we find ourselves justified in adding, that the inhabitants of the Colony in general in the same manner appreciate the success of your endeavors to maintain order, discipline, and good feeling among the members of the corps under your command. May the Almighty grant you still many years to enjoy the reminiscences of the more active periods of your life; the blessings ol bodily and mental health ; and the pleasure of seeing and knowing your numerous offspring prosperous and happy. The undersigned officers of the Brandcorps, although not having been under your immediate command, avail themselves of the present opportunity to express their cordial concurrence in the sentiments of appreciation of your conduct as Stadshauptmand, and their sympathy for your future to subscribe ourselves, > Dear and valued Sit, Vour obedient humble servants,
(Hero follow the signatures of 36 officers of the Militia and Brand Corps.) St. Croix, 1st October 1853.

REPLY. To the above address the following reply was received. To The Officers of the St. Croix Militia and Brand Corps, Gentlemen ! I hardly need assure you that I feel most thankful to all of you, for the honor you have done me, by presenting me your address of the 1st of October, which is a proof dear to my heart, that I have, by my deportment as Chief of the Militia, succeeded in securing, not only your approbation as officers of the corps, hut also your personal good will as private individuals ; and it must certainly he a source of true comfort to me, in my last days, to know that so many kind and sincere wishes accompany me on my retirement into private life, precisely on the part of those, whom 1 have had the honor of commanding for the full time of 26 years þÿ a period which I beg leave to assure you in parting 1 look hack to with feelings of unmingled pride and satisfaction. I remain, Gentlemen, Your obedient humble servant, Peter de Nuu.v. Christiansted, 10th October 1853.

The Dardanelles. þÿ The strait ol" the Dardanelles, which divides Europe from Asia, is upwards of fifty miles in length, with an average breadth of two miles. The shore on either side is f'rin ged with cypress groves, and the strait itself presents a very animated appear ancc, thousands of white-sailed caiques gliding lightly over the waves, and coming and going inces santly from shore to shore. There is a strong current setting constantly from the Sea of Marmora into the Archipelago, and this, added to the defences of the place, render the forcing of the passage by armed vessels a very hazardous undertaking. The fortifications originally consisted ot' four castles, two on the European and two on the Asiatic side. Of these two stand at the southern extremity, and two about eighteen miles further up the strait. The name Dardanelles is now especially applied to some fortifications erected in modern times between the new and the old castles, a short distance from the entrance df-the straits. The number of guns mounted on these fortifications, and some others of lesser importance, is nearly seven hundred, besides eight large mortars for throwing shells. Among tliem are several immense guns, from which stone shot are discharged. The quantity of powder which these guns require is enormous; the largest is charged with 3301 h. of powder, and throws a stone shot 8001b. or 1,0001b. weight. They are more formidable in appearance than reality, and the firing of such large pieces of ordnance is not

unattended with danger to their own artillery men. The Queen and the þÿShamrock. The Daily Express says : þÿ " It might not be amiss to mention, as an intercstinc fact connected with her Majesty's visit, that one of the royal servants brought with him to the train a sod of shamrock which had been dug up in the grounds attached to the Vice-regal Lodge. A procelain pot received the plant, which, as it had been obtained at the special request of her Majesty, is probably destin ed to be transplanted to some of the royal grounds, and cultivated as a memento of a visit which will be long memorable in Ireland."
From the Observer, September 4, 1853. THE LATE SIR C. NAPIER.

We have fallen upon evil days þÿ "Star after Star decays." The death of Wellington has been followed by the death of Napier, and England numbers one great man the less amongst her ablest defenders. Covered with honours, though not bowed down with years, the conqueror of Scinde has passed from this world ; and, in the words of the Bible, "there is a throne vacant in Israel." This great general þÿ this great administrator þÿ this great man, has, however, left behind him a name second perhaps to none, in the page of future history as a conqueror, as a statesman, and as an individual. Peace to his ashes. The public career of Sir C. Napier was, in every sense of the word, a struggle against difficulties of no common order. Too honest a man to be the tool of any Government, he was, from the independence of his opinions, almost always in opposition. He began his military life as a subaltern in 1798 ; and his first glimpse of the horrors of war was obtained in his own country, (Ireland) during the formidable rebellion ot that year. The cruelties, the atrocities, the horrors perpetrated by the soldiery and the veoiuanry at that period never passed from his memory ; and to the last hours of his life he stigmatised them in the strongest and most indignant language. Nor was he less vehement in his expressions of abhorrence on the subject of the American war, in which lie subsequently served, and with which he was speedily disgusted. In India, however, his genius had ample scope; and there he proved to the

world that he was equally great as a diplomatist, as an administrator, and as a genera), lie conquered Scinde, and annexed it to British rule ; but to this hour he is remembered with gratitude by the natives þÿ even by his old foes þÿ job the captive Ameers þÿ for his humanity and his justice. The reforms which he operated on the Indian army, are almost incredible ; and no man but he could, perhaps, have effected them. In him the Duke of Wellington found an alter ego, and Lord Ellenborough an able coadjutor. Nevertheless, while "honours" were rained upon theGoughs, the Keans, the Ilardinges, tfcc., Sir C. Napier had no reward except that which it is reserved to history to bestow upon heroes. In every sense of the word Sir C. Napier was, nevertheless, a great man ; and now that praise or censure are all alike to him, his name will ever stand prominent among the foremost illustrations of British genius, of British valour, and of British worth. Peace to his ashes !
AUSTRALIA. ("GENTEEL") LIFE AT THE DIGGINGS. " Melbourne, May 20. " After I parted with my cousin, I went up to Canvas Town with my blan-

3T» A T I 3, ket on my back, my faitli ful old dog Ben behind me, and £2 3s. in my pocket. I paid m-y 5s. for the privilege of pitching my tent þÿ namely, a blanket stretched over a pole, and a branch or two of a shrub to stop up each end þÿ and purchased a 21b. loaf, for which I paid Is. 3d., and Jib. of butter, Is. Gd. þÿ this being the price at Melbourne. At the diggings provisionsare nearly double þÿ wcare paying 3s. Gd. for a 41b. loaf; salt butter, 4s. per lb. ; fresh, Gs. Meat is cheap, Gd. per lb. I assure you £20 does not go far, and you may labour for months without finding a pennyweight of the precious metal to reward your exertions. Having refreshed myself, I retired to rest, in my blanket, as safe, in my opinion, with my dog on the look out, as if I had had a detachment of the London police, around my habitation. I slept soundly enough until morning, when 1 lay awake, turning over in mind what would be best to do in my present trying circumstances. At last I resolved to try and get a situation as a surgeon's or chemist's assistant. So I went to a warehouse, where I had left my box, and put on a suit of my best clothes, and so different did the doctor appear from the digger, that my faithful dog did not know me, and was making sundry tierce demonstrations when 1 returned to my tent ; but when 1 spoke to him it was all right, and he allowed me to enter. 1 perambulated Melbourne for many days, calling at many places, but finding no one that would take me þÿ some saying that as I was a surgeon's pupil I was

not eligible for a chemist's assistant, and others that if 1 had had my articles of apprenticeship they might have been induced to try me. At last I became so disgusted that I gave up this plan in despair. I had at this time only 15s. in the world, when, strolling down one of the streets of the city, 1 saw an advertisement for hands to redecorate the circus. I applied, and fortunately obtained a at whitewashing for 15s. a day. I worked at this four days, and earned £3, which I thought quite a little fortune, and with it 1 started in the fruit line, and made myself hoarse crying, 'Fine peaches, here, two for a shilling ; splendid apples, Gd. a-piece.' Oh dear, oh dear ! you have no idea, dear mother, by your snug fireside, to what a poor new chum may be reduced in this colony. I assure you, I saw two of the students of Guy's Hospital working on the wharf for 10s. a day. They told me they had been to the diggings, lost all their money, had no friends to help them, and had no other resource for their living ; they told me they had been working on the roads with a Fellow of one of the Oxford Colleges. I'oor fellows ! I did pity them. But, to return. 1 stuck to the fruit trade about three weeks, but could not make it answer, and quite accidentally 1 met the young man of whom I spoke to you before, and who came out in the same ship with me. lie left his situation, having saved about £5; we agreed to become partners. I took a stall in the Western Market, my

father's old friend, .Mr. IS., kindly ad vanning me £20. We bought a tent for £5, and also a small stock of goods at auctions þÿ such as boots and shoes, clothes, books, &.C., very cheap. We had to pay 20s. a week to Government for a standing in the market. The first two or three weeks we did pretty well, but at the end of that time nearly fifty new standings were added to the market. This, tremendous increase, of course, decreased our business, so that at the end of six or seven weeks we found ourselves £12 or £15 poorer than when we began ; so we came to the conclusion that we would go to the goldlields, and try our luck. Having thus decided, I obtained a promise from my partner that if 1 could obtain another loan of £20 from Mr. B., he would consider himself my debtor for £10. I did so ; and, having sold our goods and tent at a tremendous sacrifice, we started for the diggings with about £30 between us. The following diary will give you a rough idea of our life from the time of our leaving Melbourne to the present time þÿ 1853. March 25: Started from May, Melbourne; encamped at Pecle's Creek. 2Gth. þÿ Encamped near Gap Inn ; got some mushrooms, and made a good breakfast. During the day met a man with a donkey ' wot vould not go,' his wife pushing behind ; he had a large family in great distress. þÿ27th. Passed Gap Inn; overtook some boys ; encamped with them about eight nnles from Bush Inn; slept under a dray. 28th : Encamped in Black Forest; had a glorious fire; dogs wide awake looking out

for bushrangers, of whom we had serious apprehensions. While stooping to lake up a log of wood for our lire a large snake raised himself up and hissed at me. I immediately beat a retreat, and lie did the same, and so our inter view ended. 29th : Encamped a mile from Carlshun; a very cold night; made a roaring lire; blankets very wet. 30th. Encamped in a shady dell, close to a deep ravine ; great fear of serpents, but fortunately they did not pay us a visit ; in the morning performed our ablutions amid the unhallowed gaze of sundry croaking frogs, slimy lizards, and noisy crows, who regarded us with evident signs of wonder in that out-of-the-way place. 31st : Camped six miles from the diggings, in great fear of some ot Dick Turpin's fraternity, as we had a jolly tire close to the road : Ben unusu ally wide awake, as he had had no supper, we being obliged to carry water hi his pot from Crypt Gaily. April 1st Arrived at Forest Creek diggings and got our licenses ; horrified at the price of provisions; gold £3 15s. Gd. per ounce þÿ none to sell; quite at a loss where to pitch our apology for a tent. 2d : Bough t an old bark hut, very much like a vat : tent let in water like a sieve; we were just in time, for it rained very heavily soon after. 3d : Rest day, Sunday ; cleaned out our new abode ; had hard dumplings for dinner, which we thought a great treat; managed to find the chapel in the evening and heard an excellent

sermon ; had the greatest difficulty in finding our way home, the night was so perfectly dark. 4th : Commenced running a level from a hole which had been abandoned. Found the stuff very hard. Drove about two feet that afternoon. 5th: Had a day's trial at surfacing; found no gold, and gave it up. My mate lost his shovel down a water hole. 6th : Commenced sinking near the bed of the creek, went down ten feet in great hopes of a good bottom, but were disappointed. Much disturbed at night by fleas, mice, and sundry other vermin. 9th : Found gold, though in very small quantities, which gave us great hopes, nth: Rose at daybreak. Continued driving þÿ very hard work, but were rewarded by a little more of the precious metal, but not sufficient to pay expenses. 12th : More gold, but still in very small particles. 13th : Becoming quite miners þÿ begun to extend our drive right and left. 14th: Very early at work þÿ better luck þÿ washing stuff improving. About twelve o'clock we found a small pocket, got above an ounce of gold out of it, took it home, and on the strength of it treated ourselves with mutton chops and tea, smoked our pipes, contemplating our new-found treasure with great delight. Put it in a wooden match-box and hid it. 15th : Up early, worked with great spirit, and got nearly another quarter ounce. 16th : Worked with all our might, but did not get more than 2 dwt. Very tired at night. Sold our stock for £6 12s. ; bought some flour for doughboys for a treat on Sunday. 17th:

Tired out with week's work; laid in bed nearly all the morning; got up and had breakfast ; put on dinner þÿ was astonished to hear bell ring for evening service, so off we started ; got there in time to hear the sermon. Text, " To him that overcometh will I give to sit with me on my throne." Excellent discourse. Returned home very hungry, had dinner, tea, and supper en masse. 18th : Blank looks all day. No gold, no gold. 19tli: Ditto, ditto. Began to think our bole worked out þÿ left it in despair. 20th : Commenced driving another hole. Got into another drive, which very kindly saved us further trouble, as there was no gold in it. 21st: Tried another side, and found it 'no go.' Dreadfully down in the dumps. 22d : Continued driving in different directions in old holes without success. At last gave it up in disgust, and went to another hole in Golden Gully; baled out water, and got a little stuff, and found in two bucketsful more gold dust than we had in all the previous part of the week. In better spirits, hoping better things for the morrow. In going home, fell in with my old schoolfellow, J. P., who took tea with us. 23d: Taken very ill with dysentery. J. P. went with my mate as my substitute. After a few days' confinement, 1 got well enough to renew my labours. W e found by Saturday night about lOoz. of nuggets and dust, which were deposited in our tent During that night and on Sunday it poured in torrents, and I slept at J. P.'s. On Monday morning I

3 3K <0 JB H> 31 went to our famous hole, fully expecting to realise out of it that fortune for which I came so far and have suffered so much. Judge, then, of my feelings when I found the hole full of water, and its site difficult to find ; and, not seeing my mate, I went to our hut, and there I perceived by the unused bed that he had not slept at home. I feared he had fallen down a hole in the darkness of the night, and was drowned. 1 made for several days every search and inquiry for him, but in vain ; at last an old digger informed me he had seen him skulking out of the tent early in the morning, with a bundle of clothes on his shoulder ; he spoke to him, and told him his mate ! wished to see him, but he took no notice and hurried off. You may guess my joy when I heard he was living, and you may imagine my disgust, when, after making the necessary search, I found that our gold was all gone, and nearly all my clothing. Thus were my hopes and expectations again blasted. Just at this time I heard of this situation as carter at the store where J. P. is clerk, at a salary of £4 a week. I have £3 with board and lodging, and here is poor Fred., late medical student in a London hospital, driving a horse and dray about Forest Creek diggings; but nevermind, dearest mother, I am earning my own bread, and I assure you it tastes as sweet again as the bread of dependence. There is, I hope, better fortune yet in store for me. I am happy to say I have met with another school-fellow, J. W., who has proved himself a true friend to
me, and we intend, when we have saved a little money, to try our luck again at digging, till we can find gold enough to pay us for all our privations and toil."

From the St. Thomas Times , Oct. 12, 1853. THE COLONIAL LAW, Communicated.

The COLONIAL LAW lias now been for some time in operation amongst us. and the time is fast approaching for the meeting in a second session of that Assembly which was created by it. to It may not, therefore, be unprofitable enquire how far it lias answered the purpose for which it was intended, and whether that purpose would not have been more effectually carried out by a modification of the Law, such as was suggested by His Majesty himself in bis gracious do sire for the contentment of bis colonial subjects. The purpose of the Colonial Law was to afford to the Inhabitants of these Islands, through a body mainly of their own choice, a means ol laying before His Majesty and the Home Government their opinions and wishes on such part ol Danish legislation as particularly affected their interests, and it was without doubt intended that this benefit should be shared in equally and impartially by each of the Islands. That this lias not been the ease, as far as the Island of St. Thomas is con cerned, we think can hardly now he doubted by any one cognizant of the circumstances under which the prclimi naries necessary to the formation of the Council as well as the election of its Members, were effected. These circumstances we shall here briefly recapitulate. The Burgher Council of St. Thomas about the middle of 1851 was required by Government to name three citizens who might either he of its own (the Burgher Council's) body or unconnected with it, as it should deem most expedient, and who were to proceed to St.

Croix to form part of a Commission appointed for the purpose ot taking into consideration the draft ot the Law which had been proposed by the Home Government for the Colonics. F.ven at tins initiatory step it was made clearly evident that the plan of leaving hut one Council, meeting in St. Croix, for consultation on the ulluirs of the three Islands, was not calculated to afford to Si. Thomas its fair share- in the benefits of the concession. None of the Burgher Councillors themselves seem to have desired the appointment, and to make up even the small number of three, who were able and willing to absent themselves from their homes and pursuits, and cross the sea to attend to political than seven necessary no less affairs, it was different nominations. to make Again, when the members came to he voted for, two of the principal commercial gentlemen ol the place, eminently calculated to represent the interest which is all-important here, declined their elections for similar reasons.

We have no intention of depreciating the abilities or the services ol the representation which was ultimately obtained, but we must be permitted to state our opinion that in it the commercial interest of this Island had not that share to which its importance entitles it, inasmuch as it had not been able to send as members any of those whom it considered fittest for its representatives. This difficulty was foreseen as soon as the project of the law appeared, and much was said out of doors on the sublect of it, and, what is of importance His Majesty himself appears to have anticipated it, for in the very first section of the first chapter, pleased provide to he that has been graciously " On the motion of the Colonial Assembly the King may decree its division into two Assemblies, the one for St. Croix, and the other for St. Thomas and St. Johns, for the transaction of all business, or lor some particular branches, and make the provisions required by this alteration in the present law." This clause served to reconcile many to the first session of the united Colonial Council in St. Croix, believing very naturally that the first measure which should emanate from our representatives would be to avail themselves of the King's gracious permission by moving the division ot the Council according to the above extract. Nothing of the kind, however, seems to have taken place. We know not whether our representatives were troin the first of opinion that the joint founc.M suited as best, or whether Horace

made a mistake when lie wrote Cerium " rant and that in t his our day the true non ronrinum mortanl version would be. " Et ctrlnm et animum ," qui transnuine curmortanl , Ac., but we are perfectly sure that a large majority ot their constituents would very much prefer that the affairs of this Island should be discussed in an Assembly ot its own, and on its own shores. It is needless to set forth here the motives and reasons ol Ibis preference. These are ably stated in the report dated 14th January 1852, of a Committee which sat in Copenhagen for the consideration ot the project of a Colonial Law. I'his document shews an accurate knowledge and a just appreciation of our position in relation to the other Islands, and recommends þÿ among many other important and useful alterations in the Colonial Law þÿ that " Two Councils should be erected in the West India Possessions, one for St. Croix, another for St. Thomas ami St. Johns, to have the right of deliberating and advising in all legislative matters. Each of the said Colonial Councils shall independently direct all municipal affairs in the placeofthe Hurgher Councils hitherto existing, one for St. Croix, and the other for St. Thomas and St. Johns, under the control of Government." The Committee propose ten as the number of each of these bodies, eight to be elected by the people, and two appointed by the King, and it recommends that the Governor should appoint " annually a joint assembly of the Colonial Councils to deliberate on the Budget

and the annual accounts for the Colonies, and also on such matters ot importance for all the Islands as he might propose for discussion." This is the only objectionable paragraph that we have noticed in the valuable report of the Copenhagen Committee. If it be intended that the Governor should call the St. Thomas Council once a year to meet and deliberate in St. Croix, we have again the old difficulty of finding

3 IN ® members able and willing to make such a sacrifice of their private convenience for the public good, and if it be intended that the joint assemblies should take place alternately in St. Croix and St. Thomas, the difficulty would only be partially removed. It does not appear by the report that the Copenhagen Committee considered such a joint assembly of the two Councils absolutely necessary, but rather that it offered the suggestion as a compromise with the view of adopting as much as possible of the original draft of the law proposed by Government, for in in- troducing the proposal it says, " A combination of the original Government plan and our proposal might perhaps as above indicated be effected by calling a joint Council together once a year in order to discuss the financial law and other matters of great importance to these Islands." Now, we do not see what great advantage would arise from the joint discussion of the Budget or other matters of major importance to the Colonies, at least we see none at all commensurate with the inconvenience to which the members of the St. Thomas Council would be subjected by having to repair to St. Croix. The opinions of the two bodies might just as well be formed separately, and transmitted to the Home Government, when should it so happen that those opinions coincided with each other, a stronger proof would surely be afforded of the utility and propriety of any measure they might thus unite in recommending than would lie given by

the recommendation of a majority in one assembly, although that assembly might be of greater numerical strength. On the other hand, should the two Councils come to different conclusions on any point supposed to be of general interest, and transmit those opposite opinions to Denmark, the Government would have the advantage of a fuller statement of the arguments both pro and con than it would be likely to obtain from a report-adopted only on one side of the question. On the whole, it appears that there is everything to recommend a division of the Colonial Council, and we hope before long to see such a proposal made and adopted. There is much in the report which. we have thus cursorily noticed deserving serious attention, and it would be well for the Colonies that some if not all of the proposals which it contains were to be adopted. We leave it however, for the present, intending at a future time to recur to its consideration should our worthy Censor of the Press by his indulgence to these observations give encouragement to their continuation.

The following laughable incident finds its way into the " Drawer" from a Scottish journal, the Edinburgh "Guardian:" " A pretty village on the neighboring coast, frequented by summer visitors, was lately the scene of a very amusing circumstance. Taking advantage of a lovely summer-day, two young ladies betook themselves to a sequestered spot a little way up the coast, where they hoped to indulge in an unmolested bathe. " After the usual preliminary proceedings, they had just accomplished the first few dips, when, to their chagrin and consternation, they observed a young gentleman of an ' inquiring turn of mind,' seated on a neighboring rock, and evidently intensely enjoying the scene. The impertinence was aggravated by

the fact, that a powerful opera-glass was made the instrument of a more minute inspection of their aquatic evolutions. "The blushing but indignant maidens remained in the water as long as was consistent with comfort and security, in the hope that the stranger would with draw, and leave them at last to their necessary toilet, when, to their horror, he was observed to descend calmly from his elevation, divest himself of his apparel, and proceed to bathe in close proximity. " But he had strangely miscalculated the results, for the spirit of the maidens was at last aroused, and they secretly determined on a bold revenge. " With an appearance of insulted modesty, they timidly withdrew from the sea, and concealing themselves behind a hidden rock, proceeded to don their garments ; then, folding up their bathinggowns, they rushed upon the habiliments of the inquisitorial gentleman, and bore them off in triumph ! " There was a 'fix!' The unfortunate man instantly comprehended the nature ot his position. A succession of shouts and supplications followed the ladies in their flight, growing fainter and fainter as the distance increased; while our ' gentleman, ' with considerable modesty, remained in the water, evincing great agitation, and imploring restitution, at first with stentorian lungs, and subsequently in animated and appropriate gestures. " But in vain ; the insulted girls were inexorable! And as the spot was very secluded, sonic hours elapsed before he could make his situation known. Ai

length a grinning rustic made his appearance, and informed him that the 'two ladies had left his clothes with a woman at the Green, a mile off, but that she wouldn't give them up until she had been paid a pound (five dollars) for taking care of them, together with the penalty of molesting the young ladies while they were bathing!'" The penalty, adds the editor, was paid on the restitution of the garments, and the unlucky wight quietly left the village where the joke was already known, and the conduct of the damsels publicly applauded. The last that was heard of this unfortunate " Peeping Tom of Coventry," he was suffering from a severe attack of rheumatism, acquired by his prolonged bath in the water, and his journey "in puris naturalibus" overland, on Ins way home. þÿ II arpcr's Magazine .

THE BURMESE þÿWAR. PEACE OR JNO PEACE. The Friend of India thus writes on this subject : þÿ " The second Burmese war has terminated. The notification which we republish in another column announces that although the King of Ava has refused to sign any formal treaty of peace, he has found himself under the necessity of making, informally, all the concessions demanded by the Governor-General. He has pledged himself, as he stated six weeks ago, not to offer any molestation whatever to the British troops, or to invade the dominions now annexed to the British empire. He has set at . liberty all British subjects held in captivity at Ava, and ' has expressed his wish that the merchants and people of both countries should be allowed, in accordance with former friendship, to pass up and down the river for the purpose of trading.' In other words lie has conceded the free navigation of the Irrawaddy, and we presume the right of trade in every portion of his dominions. Therefore, mindful of the assurance he gave that hostilities would not be resumed so long as the Ceurt of Ava refrained from disputing our quiet possession of the province of Pegu, t he Governor-General in Council is willing to accept these pacific declarations and acts of the King as substantial proof of his acquiescence in the proposed conditions of peace, although a formal treaty has not been concluded.- The river blockade is raised, and the army of Ava will no longer be maintained upon a war establishment. All the troops compo-

sing it will receive a donation of six months' batta, which is now the established substitute for prize money, and a considerable portion of them will still remain to garrison Pegu. The forces in that province are distributed into two divisional commands, the northern, which has its headquarters at Prome, being placed under the command of Sir .1. Clieape, the victor of Donabew. The southern division, which includes the forces in Pegu Proper, and the Tenasscrim Provinces, lias been bestowed upon Brigadier-General Steele, previously in command of the Madras division of the army. A portion of the officers on staff employ have received permission to return to their posts, and the prohibition against the presence of the wives and families of officers in Pegu is removed, as far as Rangoon is concerned. This prohibition, the neglect of which has so repeatedly interfered with the operations of our armies has, we believe, been in this instance most rigidly observed, and the order will be received as a boon by scores of officers who have been separated from their wives and families for nearly a year and a half. " It is now exactly seventeen months since the insult offered by the Governor of Prome to Captain Fishbourne rendered a second war with the King of Ava inevitable. Within that time the British troops under General Godwin have broken the strength of the monarchy of Ava,

defeated the Burmese wherever they have ventured to resist their progress, and have annexed to the British dominions a country twice as large as the kingdom of Greece. Moreover, they have done all this in a country by nature almost impassable for Europeans, where almost every article of food was supplied to them from Calcutta, where climate proved itself a more deadly enemy than the hostile force, and where they were compelled to war with disease in its most enervating and discouraging form. In less than two years we have repaired thepmrtgeof our name, which had been seriously impaired by twenty years of tame submission to the insults of a court, which, though regarded by us as barbarian, was estimated by Asiatics according to its own pretensions. We have obtained possession of another of those great Asiatic deltas which teem with the luxuriant fertility of the tropics, and have opened to our traders another river, which may well be compared, in its own size and the richness of the tracts through which it flows', with the Ganges or the Indus. And we have accomplished all this at an expense which, we believe, has always been within the capacity of the regular revenue to sustain, and at a cost of human life which, though undoubtedly great, bears no comparison to that of a single European battle, and which has been diminished by every expedient science could suggest or energy secure. The Governor-General has been moderation itself. The ministry did not desire the war, the court of directors

regretted it, the public were scarcely reconciled to it, and it was denounced from the first by the English press as a quarrel about a swamp. Vet, in spite . of press, Parliament, and people, of the Board of Control, the Court of Directors, and the government of India, the red line þÿ the mark of British dominion þÿ surrounds Pegu. We have quitted the Peninsula, and are fairly embarked in the affairs of Indo-Chinese Asia, and if any one imagines the red line will remain at the 96th degree of east longitude, he has studied the history of India to exceedingly little purpose." The King of Siam, it would appear, is already pushing the conquests far into the Malayan Peninsula.

COMMUNICATION. To the Editor of the " Avis !" | Sir ! In your paper of the 23d September last, an article appeared recommending the use of a Forking Machine, to supersede the Plough. It affords me much pleasure to see some attention paid by the Press to the highly important subject of Agriculture, on which all classes of this community depend. Your remarks on the want of manual labour and other inconveniences attendant on the cultivation of sugar estates are very correct ; but in the mean time, it is absolutely necessary to devise means to overcome the difficulties with which wc have at present to contend, that is, to economise labour as much as we can in every branch attending the cultivation of the sugar cane. Experience, this year, has convinced me that it is quite unnecessary to fallow plough or bank, both operations absorb a large amount of manual and animal labour, which I consider wasted. All that is necessary in the preparation of the land prior to planting is to trench, lay in the manure and cover it with another cut of the plough, subsoil and plant in the same cut that is made in covering

the manure, leaving the space between the rows to be tilled after. After-tillage promotes the growth of the plant. On the old system with the enormous amount of manual labour expended in digging cane holes, the land was not as the above simple method. " It is no well prepared to receive the plants as by theory." I have 50 acres growing that were planted as above, which are as promising as any that were fallow ploughed. If it answers on stiff clay soils, how much better for lighter soils ? I invite all persons interested to call at Upper or Lower Love, where the pieces will be pointed out and every informatioh given. Three years ago I invited all persons interested to call and see wide planting and implemental husbandry þÿ see Nos. I and 2, Agricultural Reporters. The re suit of that system is that. Upper Love estate delivered in 1850, 159,718 lbs. sugar nett ; in 1851, 195,972 lbs. ; in 1852, 198,038 lbs. ; and in 1853, 254,098 lbs. showing a difference of 94,380 lbs. in favor of 1853 to that of 1850. Facts are stubborn things ; but this statement I trust will prove the advantage of the new system. Should my bumble efforts tend to benefit my neighbors', I have only discharged a duty that is incumbent on all, and with the hiessing of Almighty God, we may all expect to prosper, by using our best endeavors. G. J. Mudie. Estate Upper Love. N. B. The plough and other implements have saved several estates from ruin ; the same may tend to produce the like effect on the public roads. Ban-
ish the hoe and tray; use the plough, weeding machine, shovel, Ac. Ac.

Trinidad. þÿ We understand that there is now in the Press, and will immediately he published, in London, a work on behalf of the West Indies, intended as a reply to those arguments which are usually relied on by the defenders of the Act ot 1846. This work, as will be seen by the following title page, is the production of a native of this Colony : þÿ " A voice for the West ; being a reply to the arguments of the Defenders of the Apt. of 184fi By William Henry Hart, a native of Trinidad, Barrister-at-Law, London." We wish our compatriot all success in his laudable labours, and trust lie will receive from the public here that encouragement, by numerous orders for copies

of the work, which can alone indemnify him, in a pecuniary point of view, for the cost to himself at which his labors on behalf of others must necessarily be prosecuted. þÿ Port of Spain Gazette. The Grenada Observer has the following : þÿ We have advices to the 1st instant from Trinidad. A report that a fatal case of Cholera had occurred in the capital, had caused great sensation, and a special meeting of the Board of Health was quickly convened by the Governor to inquire into the circumstances of the case. " It would seem, however," says the Port of Spain Gazette, " that the case must have been a sporadic one, for no other person has been since attacked, and the Colonial Hospital, although full of sick persons, is decidedly free of cases analogous to that of Cholera. Besides, the person in question þÿ wife of Mr. Babb, tailor of this town þÿ had been ill some days." Trade continued very dull, and on the 1st instant there was but one squarerigged vessel lying in the Gulf, and she was to have sailed the next day. The Legislative Council was appointed to meet on Saturday last, when the Estimates of Expenditure and Ways and Means for 1854 would he considered.

Demerara. þÿ A correspondent of ours has lately visited the rice cultivation on plantation Vive-la-Force, and was much gratified at its appearance ; some 80 to 00 acres densely covered with this plant, bending down under large and well filled ears; it has been estimated the yield will be large, from 40 to 50 bushels per acre. The American gentleman in charge of this cultivation is ofopinion that it equals Carolina rice in quality. We have a sample lying before us, and the grain seems well shaped and of good colour. Reaping is to commence at once, and ere long, we trust, some sample bags of paddy (i. e. rice in the husk) will he on their way to Liverpool, the great rice market of the world. This, we believe, .will be the first shipment ofgrain from this country, and we shall wait with some anxiety for the report on the quality and value of this new export. þÿ Guyana Gazette. The Royal Gazette states as follows: þÿ The news of the fortnight may be very judiciously confined to the weather and the crops. Politics are no longer known among us : the lion lies down with the lamb; the distinctions of reformer and anti-reformerare no more recognised now than the atrabilarious cognomena of whig and tory, which of old used to shake England, are in the senate of the mothercountry or in political discussion. The extreme heat of the weather has caused an adjournment of the Court of Policy, and there is literally nothing doing in a political sense which can be of interest beyond the limits of the colony.

Yellow fever has again, we are sorry to say made its appearance among us : the victims being for the most part seamen and Portuguese. In the case of this last class, their own filthy and penurious habits are very much to blame both for the fever and the mortality attendant upon it. They will not pay for medical advice, and rarely reach the hospital until beyond the influence of human aid or skill. In the case of sailors, this cannot be asserted as a reason; yet the sickness and mortality among them is very great, and has given rise to doubts whether our hospital system is such as to give even the weak security, which medical skill and attendance are supposed to give, against the scourge of the tropics. There is only one experienced visiting physician to an Hospital numbering three hundred patients, and this a gentleman in extensive practice ;

3 1T% A T IT 3 while the Resident Surgeon is in almost every case, whether there be epidemics peculiar to the climate or no epidemics, a young man fresh from Europe, his experience limited to the prelections of a professor, the dressership of an Infirmary, and the demonstrations of a dissecting-room. The subject is attracting much public attention ; and, as it is quite possible the opportunity of an alteration may one of these days present itself, it will, we have little doubt be taken advantage of. The salary is a difficulty. Here, the medical man in respectable practice will not easily be induced to give his time and skill for nothing ; and he cannot, as the visiting physician of the mother country, make up by an income from pupils what he may privately lose in his practice. The experience to lie gained is not, we are afraid, a sufficient temptation. We have had a succession of heavy rains þÿ singular weather for the season of the year, þÿ but favourable to the young canes, and not seriously antagonistic to sugar-making. The heat has been intense during the day; the dews heavy and chilly in the morning. Canes are beginning to yield better. Mercantile business still continues dull ; shipping is abundant ; freights are low. The appearance of the home market and the abundance of tonnage has caused a demand for produce of all kinds, which is now selling at high rates.

From the St. Lucia Palladium, October 8. THE FRENCH IE\\1>S. The new Governor of Martinique, the Count de Gueydon, arrived at Fort de France on the 23rd September, and was received with the customary honours. On the following day His Excellency announced his assumption of the Government by a Proclamation, of which we present our readers with the following version : þÿ " Inhabitants of Martinique, þÿ Having been called by the Emperor to the honour of governing your beautiful Island, the cradle of the Empress Josephine, whose memory is dear to every Frenchman, I arrive among you full of confidence in the future, firmly resolved to labour without intermission for the realization of the great and generous views of Napoleon III., and to establish upon a new basis the only prosperity that is not ephemeral, namely, that which shews itself in the well-being and satisfaction of all.

" You may all, without distinction of of origin or class, rely upon an efficient protection, and an equal degree of patronage, on the part of the administra tion which has been confided to me. " Whatever position you may hold m the social hierarchy, a hierarchy which is no less beneficial than it is necessary and inevitable, and on that account to be respected, you must never forget that labour is your first duty ; the plough does honour to him who guides it ; labour is the attribute of the free man ; labour is the law of all ; it is the law of God. " Endeavour to suppress, by charity and christian perseverance, all licentiousness and vagabondage, those two scourges which are fostered by the recollections of the past, but proscribed by " the Catholic Religion and laws. Make me acquainted with the actual amount of your prosperity, your wants, the improvements to be introduced, and your means of cultivation and manufacture, those main elements of the Country's existence. In siiort give me your assistance : the initiative must come from us ; the protection of the Home Government will not be wanting. Under the guidance of the able Minister whom the Emperor has placed at the head of the Colonial Department, I am confident I shall succeed in developing more and more those domestic habit and that love of regular labour, which are the sure success of a prosperity that will heal all our sores, and efface even the recollection of slavery, now for ever abolished. " Your privileged climate yields some

splendid advantages : plant with an eye to the future ; your crops will ripen, and your products be brought to sale under the tutelary authority of tlie providential man who governs France, and who knows so well how to satisfy the interests of the Community at large." Count de Gueydon, Governor of Martinique. Port de France, th September, 1853. 24
