THE DYING HUSBAND. Thou art getting wan and pale, dearest; Thy blush has flown away, And thy fragile form more fragile grows Every day þÿ Every gloomy day that brings That mournful moment near When we must part, to meet no more On this dull sphere.

I feel the hour is drawing nigh When I must quit this life, And leave, I trust, fbr happier one Its scene of strife. Oh, could I steal the sting with me 'Twill bring to thy fond heart, Without one pang, or tear, or sigh, I could depart.

But oh ! it rends my bosom deep To watch thy stifled pain þÿ To see thy efforts to bear up. And smile again While , as thou raisest up my head And hang'st my pillow o'er, Thy tearful eye too plainly tells An aching core.

Ah ! little, little did I drcame The grief in store for the, When I invited thee too share My destiny. My heart, but young and hopeful then, Before me only viewed Bright hours of sunshine to divide, With roses strew'd.

IIow sadly false those hopes have proved Thy aching breast must feel þÿ Torn by affection that might break A heart of steel. Had I but known this mournful fate Ere wedded life began, No breaking heart should watch to-night A dying man.

Oh ! what a life of misery, Partner of my distress, Thy lot has been since linked with mine : Worst wretchedness. To watch me laboring for bread, My brain and hand outworn, Till prostrated by fell disease, 1 sunk forlorn.

Yet never in my fretful mood Did angry word or look Return my ill-deserved wrath With one rebuke. No ; always patient, ever fond, And bending to my will, Thy gentle spirit murmured not One word of ill.
The hour will soon arrive, my own, When I can wrong no more, And life for me, with all its cares, Will soon be o'er. I need not ask thee to forget Each word or thought unkind ;
Thy gentle mind. The little pledge that crowned our love, That smiling little elf, Dear to my heart because so like Thy own sweet self. Ay, bring her near me let me look þÿ My last in her dear face,
<© m (D a ss Where all her mother's gentle charms I fondly trace.

She will be. dearer to thee now That I am torn away. Poor infant, to be fatherless Ere one short day. But thou wilt watch and guide her steps Into a heavenward road, And lead her from this world of sin, Nearer her God.

Nay, let not all thy bitter grief Be stifled and suppressed : Weep out thy poor afflicted soul On this fond breast. 'Tis not a hopeless parting, dear þÿ We'll meet in world more bright, And live forever in those realms Of endless light.

The happiest hodrs that blessed us here Were misery and woe, Compared to those beyond this scene We yet shall know. Then live for that bright world of bliss, And feed thy drooping heart On hopes of that blrfst hour when we Shall never part.

Russian Steamers and Russian Industry. The passage þÿ from Constantinople to Odessa is effected in fifty hours by the Russian steamers, but those who are accustomed to the comfort, elegance, 1 and scrupulous cleanliness of the Mediterranean and Atlantic steamers will be horrified when they find themselves on board a Russian vessel. It is impossible to express the filth and disorder they present, the deck being heaped with provisions and goods, and crowded with a disgusting mob of mendicant Turks, pilgrims, Jews, and Russian or Cossack women. There are in Russia two great branches of manufacturing industry : the first is that which employs the raw materials furnished by the soil, such as iron, copper, and other metals. The Ural chain, from whence these arc principally derived, is one of the most remarkable mountain ranges in the world
weal th. To say nothing of its gold, silver, and platina ores, the iron of Sibe-

The other branch is manufactures of woollen cloths, silks, and these, although supported by the Government, have in many cases turned out failures, as Russia is of entering into competition with the manufactures of western Europe. It is estimated that of the vast population of the empire only three millions are nobles or tradesmen, and all the classes below these arc utterly incapable of becoming customers of the expensive manufactories established in Russia. Travelling Thy loving heart I know too well þÿ would nowhere be better conducted than Dollars per annum, payable Paper in Russia if the posting houses were better conducted, and more punctual in supplying horses. The country is perfectly flat, and the traveller may proceed received several hundred leagues without meeting a single hill. Besides this, the Russian driver has no mercy on his horses ; they must gallop continually should they days.

drop dead under the whip. The post houses seldom afford anything beyond hot water for tea and a bench to rest upon, so that without a supply of provisions and other necessaries travellers would be reduced to the greatest straits- Kherson, once a place of great opulence and importance, is now inhabited almost exclusively by Jews. Nothing can be more hideous than the appearance ot the Russian Jews, dressed in a uniform garb consisting of a long robe of black calico, fastened with a woollen girdle, canvas drawers, and a broad-brimmed black hat, they all present so degraded a type of humanity that the eye turns from them with disgust.

Domestic Economy. þÿ By means of stoves a high temperature is preserved in all houses in Russia, even during the most rigorous winter. For more than ten months the outer air is never admitted into the houses, and strangers are affected with an uneasy sense of oppression and torpor. To this cause must be attributed the total absence of bloom or freshness from the cheeks of the Russian ladies. They are incapable of enduring the slightest change of temperature, and have no idea of the pleasure derived from inhaling the fresh air. But for dancing, of which they are passionately fond, their lives would pass away in almost absolute immobility. What the stranger finds it most difficult to ac custom himself to in Russia is, the horrible sheepskins in which men, women, and children are muffled at all times of the year. These half-tanned skins, which arc worn with the wool inside, give them a savage appearance, which I is increased in the men by the long beard and moustache they invariably wear The women labour much in the field, and generally marry between fifteen and sixteen, becoming old by the time they are thirty. Whether a Russian woman's age be fifteen, twenty, or thirty, it is all one in the end ; immediately after childhood her limbs are as masculine, her for the extent and variety of its mineral ! features as hard, her skin as tanned, and her voice as rough as at a more mature age. among the peasantry ; and most of the cottons ; but I young women are as much addicted to them as the old. I'll is will be a memorable day dotlblv memo þÿ ruble þÿ memorable for the opening of the most magnificent spectacle ever exhibited on the American Continent, and memorable for the public reception in our midst of the President þÿid the I nited States, and the highest functionaries of our tiovernment. It is a jubilee þÿ in a sense a universal jubilee, for men have come to mingle in it not simply from every State in this Federal liiion, but from every civilized nation, and every inhabited clime under heaven. They have come not by scores or by hundreds, but by thousands and tens of thousands. They have come with warm hands and open hearts, eager with interest, bright with hope, to see with their own eyes all that is to be seen, and to hear with their own cars all that is to lie heard. It is a jubilee of thought not of' merriment þÿ of industry not of idleness þÿ of permanent ideas not of ephemeral feelings þÿ of an age of business and not an age of shows. It is a jubilee such as belongs peculiarly to the soil of þÿfreedom such as allows of neither passports nor cordons þÿ such as stirs the pulse, braces the muscles, illumines the understanding, and fires the þÿsoul such as sets in action free thought and free speech þÿ such as the enslaved are incapable of, and the misgoverned unfit for þÿ such as England and America alone of the tuitions dare summon into actual existence

3 tr 3 Ji b 'i x ; a t fhe Exhibition opens under cheering and noble auspices. As that of England was inaugurated by the Queen, þÿ the impersonation of the power and majesty of the kingdom þÿ so is this by the President, the representative of the Union of the States, and the sovereignty id' the people. Hut the two enterprises, though finally crowned with the same success, earned it by very different kinds ol effort. The English Exhibition from the outset was a government undertaking, Prince Albert conceived it and Parliament supplied its funds All the t'cjtil that royalty could bestow upon it, all the furtherance that the Foreign office could give it, þÿ were þÿQueen þ s ÿCommissioners, and the lloyal it had from the outset. Its managers Societies its regular councillors. The national honor of England was involved in it, and the eyes of the world were bent upon it, from the beginning. 'fhe American Exhibition, on the other hand, has been purely a private undertaking. It was planned by private citizens, supported by private funds, managed in all its departments by private agencies. Its objects indeed were in some important respects facilitated by our City, our State, and our General Government, but by no means to an extent that took away any of its qualities as a private enterprise. It met with constant difficulties at its earlier stage, and none greater than the general indifference with which it was regarded. Hut it gradually commanded attention, inspired confidence, prevailed over embarrassments, extended and perfected its system

of operations, and now this day presents itself before the country and the world, a proud proof of American energy and skill, a work worthy of þÿearth foremost s empire. These exhibitions are of stirring interests as showing the mastery of mind over matter, but they are of vastly more consequence as creating an affinity between mind and mind aud between soul and soul. They bring the most active and j thoughtful men of all nations into contact to an extent and with a mutual regard that could not possibly be secured by any other means. They display the real community of interests, and quicken the sense of universal brotherhood. They make industry more respected, peace more secure, freedom more familiar. It is not too much to say that the lessons which will be learned by the thousands of the continental Europeans, who will be brought to our shores by this great spectacle, will be worth more to the cause of rational freedom and true progress in Europe than a dozen campaigns under any tri-color that ever floated Foreign countries which have always contemplated our institutions at a dim distance, will now through the most intelligent of messengers be made to obtain a better appreciation ol their character and fruits. The Crystal Palace is not the only nor the main exhibition that will be presented to the eyes of the strangers that flock to our shores. The spectacle which will a thousand times more amaze these men who have learned to despise the Kepubliean name, is the liepublic itself þÿ A \ Courier mot Jyiiqiurrr,

Now, what is the condition of the building What are the arrangements lor the day t To begin with the Palace a great amount of labor was yesterday accomplished, within this beehive of human industry. The "AVIS." ( 'hristia listed , Friday the ftth August 1853. Insurrection in Torlola.

We learn that intelligence lias been received by the Commandant of St. Thomas, from the President of the V irgin Islands, Colonel Chads, that an Insurrection broke out in Tortola on Monday last the 1st instant, in consequence of a newly enacted law, in levying a tax on the cattle, and that the labourers the country on same day had threatened to attack the town On Tuesday evening, and later in the night, several boats with fugitives, most of whom were women, including Colonel Chads' family, arrived at St Thomas, and communicated the intelligence that the town was destroyed by tire, a few constables wounded, and several negroes shot. The President remained in the Island. The Commandant of St. Thomas immediately despatched a schooner to Tortola with a small force, consisting of 1 officer and 30 men, with orders to touch at the bays, and render assistance to those persons who may be in want of opportunity to leave the Island. The Government here, after receiving an account of the Insurrection, on the evening of the 3d, gave orders that the Government Schooner Vigilant should be immediately despatched to St. Thomas with a force of 1 officer and 30 men, to be placed at the disposal of the Commandant. This, however, was not effected before yesterday morning, (the 4th) as the Schooner was in the lload of Frederiksted. The Commandant of St. Thomas has been further instructed to place the detachment already sent to Tortola under the immediate disposal of Colonel Chads, until the

latter should deem the presence of that force unnecessary. We await, with anxiety, further details of this Insurrection. From the dilapidated state of most of the houses in the town, we fear that the devouring element must have left very little property to be rescued from the hands of the rabble.
We trust, however, that the small force despatched from St. Thomas may arrive in time to save whatever lives may be in danger.

To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis ! ruffianly writer who signs himself " A Sir, þÿ The profligate production of the Friend to the Insulted" has not failed to create it painful sensation in the mind of every one who possesses a true sense ol morality and piety. What are we to infer from the rabid and vulgar outpourings of it writer who dares to head bis article with one of the most heart-stirring appeals from Man to bis Creator, and ass couples " it with such assinine " a liar " animal" terms of " very yet <fcc. ? And if such, as it is evident, is his sense of religion, his veneration for bis Maker, his respect for public opinion, þÿ what justice, what consideration, what regard can mortal expect at bis hands? Can it, therefore, be surprising, that the writer calumniates Veritas? He accuses Veritas of having coolly digested a lie þÿ without adducing the least proofofit. I dare him, nay provoke him to prove his false assertion. Let him explicitly state at what time, in what place, in what paper the lie was given. While be proclaims from the housetop the cowardliness of Veritas' "incognito," he yet unblushingly writes anonymously. Was Junius a coward? Was Scott a coward ? But "A Friend" is of opinion yes, for bis own act and words prove him to be both a coward and hypocrite. He pretends to see the mote in bis brother's eye, but not the beam in bis own ! He thanks God that he is not even like unto the Publican, and yet shows such a rottenness of mind that that of the sepulchre pales in insig-

nificance before it ! But, Sir, of what avail can it be to preach Gospel truth to a being who betrays such feelings of immorality and irreligion ? "A Friend to the Insulted" denies flatly, that the petition undervalues the services of the Brandcorps at the two last fires. 1 provoke him to publish a copy of the petition, in order that the public may judge between him and Veritas ; in order that they may see which of the parties has asserted the thing that is not. Absurd as the insinuation is, that Veritas advocates Socialism and non-advancement ! it is yet worthy of some notice as it portrays the character of "a Friend," who may well be called "The Dog Fiend." Having engendered in his mind a quantity ofgall and venom he bespatters both friends and foes alike. His distinction between socialism and advancement is very clever, for a madman. In conclusion, Sir, I beg to state in the words of a celebrated author, that the public may be deceived in their opinion, but in their estimation of men and things never ; and I am convinced, that Veritas' good name and moral worth stand too high to be contaminated by the slanderous breath of such beings as " A friend to the Insulted" or " the Dog Fiend." I am, Sir, Yours truly, Pim.o Veritas.

TOPICS OF THE DAY. No man who thinks at all can hesitate as to the peril to which a Russian possession of Constantinople would expose English interests, and the general balance of European power ; and we are certainly as deeply interested as any European state in endeavouring to prevent, even by the last resort, such a contingency. Rut England is much more interested in the power that is to hold the keys of the Raltic, the mouth of the Elbe, and the harbour of Kiel ; and in the light of .resent events on the Dardanelles, we cannot but regard future contingencies in the Sound as deserving of more attention than they have recently met with from the English public, and as by no means satisfactorily disposed of by the answers Lord Beaumont obtained last Friday, or by the treaty of the 8th May 1852. We are not going into the genealogical and legal mazes of the Schleswig-IIolstein question. Enough is stated for the English public in repeating, that the treaty of May 1852 guarantees the succession of the entire Danish kingdom, on the approaching extinction of the male Hue of Denmark, to Prince Christian of Glueksburg and his issue by Louisa of Ilessc, niece of the late and cousin of the present King of Denmark. Russia is a party to this treaty, and the Emperor has renewed in favour of Prince Christian and his issue the renunciation made by the Emperor Paul of a portion of the Duchy of llolstein that would revert to him on failure of the male line in Denmark. It is this renunciation that Lords Clarendon and Malmcsbury lay so much stress

upon in their replies to Lord Beaumont. Russia might have claimed her territory in Holstcin, and she has given it up þÿ what better proof of disinterested desire for the peace of Denmark and the tranquillity of Europe ? Perhaps the public will estimate the disinterestedness of Russia less highly when it learns that by this same treaty twenty persons arc passed over whose rights intervened between the Danish crown and the Russian royal family as descended from Duke Adolph of (lottorp ; by which means Russia's heirship general to the Danish crown becomes a far more valuable reversion, while in the mean time she consolidates and confirms her influence in Denmark by a seeming act of generosity, and by being a party to the guarantee. What is really important is, that, after the precedent of the treaty of Utrecht, an absolute renunciation should be obtained from the Emperor of Russia, for himself and his descendants, of all claim to the Danish crown, þÿ a stipulation guaranteed by all the powers of Europe that the already gigantic power of Russia shall not be rendered more dangerous to Europe than at present by the possession of Denmark and the Duchies, and with them the power of closing the Baltic and of passing thence at pleasure. It may be said that it will be time to raise this question when the realization of Russia's reversion is imminent. We reply, in the first place, that this treaty of May 1852 renders it more imminent by the removal of twenty competitors ; and that

were it a more remote and impossible event than it appears to us at all prudent to regard it, it would yet be incumbent on that Europe which thought years of bloody and expensive conflict not too high a price to pay for the permanent severance of the crowns of France and Spain, to take such precautionary measures as may prevent the necessity in a similar case of having recourse to similar means. We take for granted that Europe never will submit to see Denmark united to the crown of Russia, as we know that England could not submit to it without endangering her commerce, her honour, and her very national existence. Why, then, should not the opportunity of a new settlement of the Danish crown have been made the occasion of embodying in the public law of Europe a satis-

3 V, <Q & ® 2L A T & factory guarantee on this most important point ? Why, indeed, except that Russian diplomacy is more able, and English diplomacy more stupid, than that of any other great country ! We trust that this question will not be allowed to rest, and that members of both Houses will refuse to be put off by the unsatisfactory refusal of Ministers to give publicity to the important correspondence that motived the treaty. The affair is not settled, as Lord Clarendon superciliously stated. The Danish Diet has refused to sanction the settlement, and has been dissolved in consequence. A new Diet is in course of election, and may chance to be equally refractory. In any case, the Duchies are not represented in the Danish Diet, and they will only submit to the proposed arrangement if overborne by force, or menaced with the compulsion of the powers that are parties to the treaty of May : they might resist Denmark, but must of course yield to banded Europe. Will England bo a party to forcing her diplomatic arrangements upon a reluctant people, and that to subserve the ambition and intrigues of Russia ? If the Government should be so disposed, will the House of Commons, little interest as it generally takes in foreign affairs, submit to have the power and influence of our country so abused ? The question is not one which concerns merely the pretensions of foreign royal families, but the vital interests of the English nation. þÿ T4c Spectator.

E. the President, and the sccoud to the Secretary of the Interior, Scnor Doctor 1'io Ceballos. The result of which is, that on the 15th inst., about two o'clock p. m., Cumana was visited by an Earthquake, the violence of which caused the destruction of a great number of the edifices in that city. The letters alluded to, refer to three persons who had arrived in Barcelona from the seat of the incident, who affirm that the whole eity has suffered, from the quarter towards the bridge and fortress of Han Antonio, situated in the Valley, as well as the bridge anil other quarters nearer to the harbour or the side towards the sea. It is also announced, that about Eight Hundred persons remain buried under the ruins. It may result, that this estimate is exaggerated ; in the first moments of a disaster it is not possible to ascertain the number of victims ; but it is conceived that the ravages must have been considerable, when we arc informed that Colonel Ramon

l'erez, with the Company of Artillery, have perished in their quarters. Senor Estanislao llendon, one of the members ol' the Provisional Government of the dissenting province, received a severe wound on the head. Colonel Jose del Carmen Guevara, another member of the Provisional Government, has been taken from the ruins. The Licicnciate Matias Loyera, member of the

Superior Court, remains exposed to the danger of losing one of his legs. Messrs. Jose Cazarcs and llumoa Ccntcno, it is affirmed, have been extricated, also injured. The letters state that in the narrow streets great many persons perished Cumana is in so calamitous a condition that there was a scarcity of provisions. It is also said that Commandant Carrero was awaiting the arrival of troops from Carupano to Cumana: that the Schooner of-war Boliear, be longing to the federalists, had arrived in that port with muskets : that Scnor Jose del llosario Armas who assumed the title of General in tiie faction in 1849, had arrived from the Island of Trinidad : that Colonel Brito had marched on tin 14th for Cumanacoa for the purpose of stifling the contra revolutionary movement of Juan Cordero : that the chiefs of the Province of Cumana had dispatched orders to him to suspend hostilities ; and that similar orders had been expedited to Margarita, where according to this intelligence, there are insurrectionary forces who yet act against the authority of the Government There are persons who believe that the consternation produced by a few deaths has excited the minds of those who sallied forth from Cumana in quest of assistance, and caused them to judge the disaster more considerable than what it may in reality be, considering that in the aggregate the principal portion of the houses in Cumana arc of wood, and from this circumstance, it is not probable that almost all the houses in the City have

been thrown down as it is announced Wo hope that the result will show the exagge ration of the report, but we apprehend great 1) that what has been published will prove a cala mitous reality. In cither case the authorities of the province of Barcelona have complied with the duties demanded by afflicted humanity. Provisions have been immediately dispatched to the scat of the disaster, and additional assistance, yet more important, was in course of preparation. General Geraldo Monagas marched from Santa Fe with two thousand men tor the purpose of occupying peaceably the ruined city, supported at. the same time by another column, consisting of two hundred men, under the command of Scnor Juan J. Valcnilla. The first and second Chiefs of the Army wore acting in conjunction for the 15th, against Maturin. Several Cumancses actually in the City, ou the roe ipt of this intelligence, have gone to La Guayra; where, it is said, they will embark in the steamer Bertha , of the national squadron, which will sail for Cuinana with other armed vessels, having on board one or two thousand men. If the misfortune proves to be such as it is announced, from this moment we indicate the idea of establishing a subscription throughout the Republic to relieve partly the misfortunes of the afflicted population. Venezuelans and strangers will undoubtedly hasten to contribute to this work, each according to its means. Persuaded, as we are, that all the opinions, all the parties, will unite for this paternal sentiment. The hos-

The city of Cumana has experienced at different times many earthquakes. On the 21st ol October, 177ti, the city was subject to many shocks by which it was destroyed, causing the death of a great number of the inhabitants ; the earth continued trembling hourly during fourteen months. On the 10th of September, 1794, there

was iii earthquake, and ou the 1 1th of December, 1797, it was again destroyed, by the falling of almost all the buildings which were of mason work On the 14th of August, 1802, and 27th of January, 1 soy, there were earthquakes, the last of which was on the 12th of April, 1839, which eaused great ravages of the buildings, but without any deaths among the inhabitants. Owing to the melancholy effects of these earthquakes, Oumana does not possess any remarkable edifices. All the houses are very slightly built, and are low, the inhabitants finding themselves compelled to sacrifice beauty for security.

The l-Teitcli Colonics. Proclamation of Admiral VAILLANT, Governor of Martinique. Inhabitants of Martinique ! þÿ Since my arrival among you, the Colony has experienced seasons of great affliction. A cruel epidemic ofYcllow Fever has caused numerous victims. We have also gone through difficult trials; for when 1 had the honor to assume the Government of Martinique, she was then deeply trembling under severe political agitations þÿ commerce was alarmed, the collection of imposts slow and difficult ; property was depreciated, and hope, which gives to man its veritable value by sustaining his courage, had abandoned in reality many breasts. To-day, how different is our situation ! The most profound tranquility and security reign every where. Property has regained its high value; commerce and agriculture have taken a greater scope ; and the easy and abundant rescripts of the þÿimposts consequences of the energetic, but equitable measures which 1 have prescribed towards all the contributors þÿ is one of the most certain indications. The financial position of the Colony is so much improved within two years, that, although the budget of the expenses of 1852 had been augmented in comparison with the preceding budget, and that of 1853 surpassed that of 1852, there has been an excess of receipts over the expenses þÿ from thence a considerable balance in the reserve of the treasury, which, for six years, remained empty. Martinique exported in 1852 more than 53,000 hogsheads Sugar ; of in 1853, she has

produced at least as much, and the quantity of standing canes which cover the soil so þÿ very productive of our beautiful colony, þÿ offers the best grounds to hope that the crop of 1854 will be yet far more valuable. In 1852, the commercial undertakings of Martinique attained the sum of 40 millions of francs, of which 25,625.000fs. were for the purpose of importations a fact not exhibited þÿ since 1818. The public works have been extended with activity; the sacred edifices have been completed and repaired ; the obstacles have been temoved from the entrance of the canals which have been dug ; all the bridges have been repaired ; the labor on the public roads have been conducted with great activity; the establishment of the harbour of ilasse- I'ointe, and the erection of Lighthouses, are in progress or completed ; the fortifications and all the means for the defence of the colony arc completed or on the point of being so.

8 'X. i'T I 3. A School of Art and Mechanics, and a refuge for young female orphans of the poorer classes, have been founded. The school of agriculture recently established will be opened before the end of the year. The benefits of gratuitous primary instruction for the children of the poor of both sexes have been multiplied by the establishment of schools in the communes which were deprived. The charitable regimen has been improved, and civil asylums are about to be established in "1 rinite," and at " Saint Esprit.'1 The prisons have become the effectual means of confinement and punishment; their regimen has been completely modified and rendered moral ; a private establishment for the reform of youthful prisoners has been created ; the cadastre has been instituted, and the labour which I had ordained relative to the mortgage debt towards giving to the properties their real value is about being completed. Agriculture has received a new impulse, owing to the honorary rewards granted to the adults and to the children employed in field labor. The Asiatic immigration, practically tested for the field cultivation, gives, on all points of the colony, the most satisfactory results. The Committee of Agriculture will, in a few days, be established; and the Dectee which 1 issued last year for the improvement and increase of animals of the cattle kind, which have in great part been destroyed after the events of 1848, offers already the most happy results. All these favors, Inhabitants of Martinique,

you owe then to the powerful and firm hand which has preserved France from the wreck wherein she was about to perish. 1 am only proud of having been selected by the Emperor to realize, in Martinique, his generous ideas. Ministers of the Lord! þÿ You whose holy prayers have called the benedictions of the Almighty on our dear colony ; And you, Magistrates, Mayors, and Members of the Municipal Councils; You, Functionaries, civil and military, who have incesssantly lent your intelligent co-operation, active and devoted for the accomplishment of the honorable mission which the Empetor lias thought proper to confide to me, receive my adieu and my affectionate thanks. Inhabitants of Martinique; þÿ At the moment when recalled to France by the Emperor to re-establish my health, I am going to separate myself from you; I cariy as a reward of my arduous labours, and of my incessant devotion to your happiness and your interest, the previous testimony of your affection and of your sympathy, which have not ceased during my administration to assuage my laborious task. The remembrance will be always dear to my heart, and binds me for ever to you and to our dear and beautiful Colony, for whose prosperity 1 shall never cease to express my vows. Fort do France, 6th July, 1853. A. VAILLANT, Hear- Admiral, Governor of Martinique, and Commander-in-Chief of the French Naval Division of the Antilles.

Christian sled, Tuesday the 9th August 1853. on Sunday morning last from Tortola, brought The Schooner þÿ Seholten which arrived here þÿ, despatches to the Government from the President, soliciting further assistance, as the rioters yet continued their depredations with fearless audacity. We learn by her that the detachment sent from St. Thomas, under the command of Baron Rosenkramtz, had reached Tortola on AVednesday evening at about 7 þÿo clock. The President came down to the beach and told them that the rebels having done their work of destruction in the town, they had retired to the country'. The troops landed very early the next morning with their luggage, stores <j-c ; and took up their position at the Government House and the School House attached to the Episoopal Church. The Schooner was despatched in the noon by the Government, with a reinforcement of 40 men and 2 cspingoles, under the command of Capt. v. Meincke ; with ammunition, i(-c . , and stores for 5 days. The Danish Troops now in that Island amount to 93 men, including three officers : Capt. v. Meincke, Lieut. Baron v. Rosenkuantz, and Lieut. P. v. Bt'GEi, ; with 2 howitzers and 2 cspingoles. We understand a physician is also sent from St. Thomas. We hope that with this force the President will be able to put down the Rebellion ; and restore order and tranquility. We await with all anxiety further intelligence.

Sir, þÿ I have the painful task to announce the sad intelligence of a disastrous Outbreak among the population of Tortola ; the destruction of almost all the buildings in þÿ Road Town the loss of several lives and considerable property ! It is difficult at this moment to collect, amidst the general excitement, from the fugitives who are arriving here at every moment, a correct statement of the full extent of the disaster, or the causes, which have led to such a fearful demonstration. It appears that the Assembly adopted a law which established an additional tax on cattle of twelve and a half cents to that of Twenty Four cents, which existed heretofore ; hence the reported pretext for a manifestation of the worst character, and involving the ruin of many7 persons. On T nesday morning intelligence was brought here, that the country labourers had evinced symptoms of disorder, by ignoring the power of the authorities, and expressing the determination to destroy the town by firing it before evening. At 9 þÿo clockin the evening by the arrival of | several boats, containing many fugitives and some wounded persons, we received the confirmation of the catastrophe, and of the savage ferocity with which the rioters attacked it, indiscriminately the properties and persons of the unoffending individuals, by setting fire to the buildings, ten of which it was then stated as having been destroyed. A sloop also came to anchor, having on board some of the members belonging to the fami-

ly of Colonel Chads. On Wednesday morning, by the arrival of some of the fugitives, the destruction of the town was announced, together with the lawless conduct of the incendiaries, and the reported loss of several lives. It is also stated that an attempt was made in the first instance to organise a force to check the progress of the rioters ; that about 25 men had been collected, but owing to their inconsiderable number, it could not be made available. The rioters attacked the gaol, broke into the public store-room, and plundered the arms. Three þÿo clock p. m. Mr. Jordan, the Wesleyan minister, has just arrived ; the excitement among the rioters is said to have reached the highest pitch. The Packet Seholten was dispatched by Government this morning (9 þÿo clock) to Tortola, with a detachment consisting of 30 soldiers, under the command of Baron Rosenkuantz. The wind being light, it is pro- I sinned, that this vessel will have reached her desj tination about t! þÿo clock.

St. Thomas, 3d August 1853. Eitrllipi' Particular ! ! The Danish Packet Schooner þÿ General ran Seholten þÿ returned here this morning from Tortola with many fugitives, who availed themselves of that opportunity to escape from the scene of distress and desolation. Owing to light winds the Seholten did not arrive in Tortola in time to enable the Military Force sent from this to oppose the action of the rioters, which resulted in considerable loss of property. The statement received announces the continuance of the excitement and exasperation among the labourers, who have expressed their determination to destroy the remaining buildings which had been spared in their late attacks. In consequence of the unfavourable aspect of things, the authorities have dispatched the British schooner þÿ Aldebaþÿron with a reinforcement of soldiers and two pieces of artillery. The threatened attack was announced to be put into execution to-day, (Saturday.) I P this information unfortunately proves correct, it is very doubtful that this reinforcement will arrive in time to afford the aid which may be necessary to the first detachment, to repel effectually the movements of the depredators, whose number is said to be from one thousand to fifteen hundred. Prince Gortschakoff, the Russian com mandcr-in-chicf of the invading armies, has addressed the following proclamation to the inhabitants of Moldavia and Wallachia: þÿ His Majesty the Emperor, my august lord and master, has ordered me to occupy your country with the armies the command of which he has deigned to confide to me. W e come among you neither with projects of conquest nor with the intention to modify the institutions under which you live, or the political position which solemn treaties have guaranteed to you. The provisional occupation of the Principalities which I am ordered to effect is for no other purpose than that of an immediate and efficacious protection in grave and unforeseen circumstances, when the Ottoman Government, distrusting the numerous proofs of a sincere alliance which the Imperial Court has never ceased to give it since the conclusion of the treaty of Adrianople, replies to our most equitable proposals with refusals, and opposes the most offensive suspicions to our disinterested advice. In his magnanimity, in his constant desire to maintain peace in the East as well as in Europe, the Emperor will avoid an aggressive war against Turkey, so long as his dignity and the interests of his empire shall permit him to do so. On the day on which he obtains the reparation which is due to him, and the guarantee which he has a right to claim for the future, his troops shall return within the frontiers of Russia. cute an order of his Imperial Majesty in declaring to you that the presence of his þÿMajesty s troops in your country shall not impose on you any fresh charges or contributions ; that the forage and rations for the troops shall in due time, and at a rate appointed and agreed on in advance by your Governments, he paid for from our military treasury. and commercial speculations ! Be obedient to the laws under which you live, and to t lie established authorities. It is by the faithful discharge of best that you will acquire the these duties claim to the generous solicitude and the powerful protection of his Majesty the Emþÿperor. þÿ Ibid.

Tlic Fleets in Itcsika Ray. From Malta we have intelligence of the fleets in Besika Bay. The English fleet, under Admiral Dundas, which left Malta at 3 a. m. on the 8th of June, was carried by a fine westerly breeze until within 90 miles of Cape Matapan, by noon on the 10th, when the steamers were employed to tow the sailing vessels, and thus the fleet reached the anchorage at Besika at eight a. m. on the 13th, exactly five days from Malta. The French fleet , under the command of Vice- Admiral de la Susse, joined it there on the 15th. The ships of both fleets were allowed to ride at single anchor, and officers going on shore on leave had strict injunctions not to lose sight of their respective ships, so that they could get under weigh at a quarter of an þÿhour s notice. It was rumoured amongst the officers that the Caradoc which had just arrived from Constantinople had brought the proper firmans for the entry, incase of need, of the passage of the Dardanelles. The naval forces united at Besika Bay ire thus composed : þÿ British. þÿ Ships of the line: Britannia, Hag-ship of Vice-Admiral Dundas, 120 guns; Trafalgar, 120; Albion, 90; Vengeance, 84; Bellerophon, 78. Frigate; Arethusa, 50 guns. Steam Frigates : Retribution, 28 guns ; Sampson 1(5; Firebrand, 6; Tiger, 16. Steam corvettes: Niger, 16 guns; Furious, 16; Fury, 6; Inflexible, 6; Wasp, 14; Modesto, 18. Steam packet : Caradoc, 2 guns. Total, 18 vessels; 776 guns. French. þÿ Ships of the line : Ville de Paris, flag-ship of Vice-Admiral de la

Sussc, 112 guns; Valmy, 120. Steam ships of the line : Montebello, 120 guns; Henry IV., 100; Napoleon 90; Bayard, 90; Charlemagne 80. Ship of the line ; Jupiter, 80 guns. Steam frigates: Mogador, guns; 16 Sane, 14; Magellan, 14. Steam corvette : Caton, 6 guns. Despatch Steamer: Chaptal, 2 guns. Total, 13 vessels ; 844 guns. The Turkish lleet is enumerated at the northern extremity of the Bosphorus, from Therapia to the Black Sea. It is composed of 35 ships, two of them three-deckers, three two-deckers, ten frigates, four corvettes, eight brigs, and eight steamers, four of which are of large dimensions. The most important part of the fleet is at anchor opposite the villages of Buyukdere and Sari-yeri. Shortly after the union of the English and French fleets at Besika Bay, Admiral Dundas with his captains paid a visit to Admiral de la Susse, and invited him with all his commanders to a grand dinner, to he given on the 20th. þÿ Ibid.

The " AVIS." Christiansted, Friday the 1 2th August 1853. We learn that the British Steamer Magdalena landed some F.nglish Troops in Tortola on the 9th instant, consisting of 93 men and 5 officers, detachments of the 67th and 2nd W. I. Infantry Regiments, from Antigua.

Intelligence has been received from St. Thomas of the extreme destitution of the unfortunate fugitives from Tortola ; many of whom, we understand, arrived almost in a state of nudity, and possess not even the necessary means to save them from starvation. The community of this Island cannot but sympathise with these unfortunate individuals, not only from experience, being almost similarly situated in 1848, but from feelings of charity which should actuate our breasts as fellow-christians. We are confident that no urgent appeals are necessary to stimulate the members of this charitably disposed community to give all the assistance which they may have in their power to render. It is therefore with pleasure we inform our readers, that a subscription is about being raised for the relief of the sufferers, and that the amount collected will be placed at the disposal of Reverend Tidemand, St. Thomas, to be distributed by him among the most destitute. Subscription lists are open at the Agency of the St. Thomas Bank in this town ; and at the office of Major Cyli.icu in Frcderiksted. The smallest subscriptions are kindly solicited.
New York Steam Line; St. Thomas Slip; and Do,-/; Accommodation.
We arc authorised to contradict the reports of the Grenada Gazette and the St. Kitts Gazette , that the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company have resolved to establish a line of steamers be-

twecn Saint Thomas and New York. We here quote the article from the St. Kitts paper : " The Dec steamer is to leave St. Thomas the þÿ 18th instant for New York, in pursuance of a resolution of the R. M. S. Packet Company, to establish a monthly communication between St. Thomas and New York, as we learn from our Confrere of the Grenada Gazette. We congratulate the sojourners in these Colonies on this highly beneficial arrangement. We further learn that the fares are 70 dollars, or Return Ticket 120 dollars. The future activity of this Company will, we confidently hope, totally efface the memory of its past supineness. Surely we now have evidence of waking from slumber. This route will find employment for those ships of the Company, that have hitherto marred the regularity of the Mail deliveries, and arc now replaced by vessels of greater power." The Grenada paper states þÿ " The West India Mail Company have established a monthly communication between Saint Thomas and New York. The Dec will leave Saint Thomas for New York on the 18th instant. Fares from St. Thomas to New York, seventy dollars, or return Ticket 120 dollars." This mistake has no doubt originated from the Dee steamer having been sent to New York for the purpose of being coppered, Ac., because the Patent Slip at this place could not take her up. In fact the Slip Company would not undertake, the other day, to take up the small steamer Derwent, there being neither depth of water or length of cradle for even such a small vessel ; þÿ

the only steamers of the Company which can be taken on the Slip being the Eagle and Esk. The Derwent also had to go as far as New York to be coppered a short time ago þÿ -and we believe the Medway will soon have to leave the West Indies for the same purpose. On this subject we are led to throw out a hint to both þÿCompanies first to the Slip Company, that perhaps it might be worth its while to raise funds to make the Slip capable of taking up large ships, as this is the class of vessels to make the concern pay. Now, the few small Crafts taken up may pay the mortgage off, <j-c., but as to its ever paying interest to the Shareholders, as it now stands, we very much doubt, because when the debts are all cleared off, the Rails may want an overhaul, Ac- Next ; if the Patent Slip Company can not, or will not, go ahead a little, it might be well worth the Mail Companies while to send for a Floating Dry Dock , such as is at present in use at Savannah, which can admit vessels measuring in length 235 feet, and breadth 60 feet, the rates for Dockage being only 35 cents per ton for the first 24 hours, and 9 cents per ton, per day afterwards þÿ the depth of the Dock being 21 i feet, breadth 68 feet, and length 240 feet. This leads us to throw out another hint, which is, that it might be well worth the while of a few of our monicd residents to take this Floating Dry Dock project into their own hands, as we believe the original cost is not very great, and has very little expense attached to its maintenance, there

only being a small steam engine erected at one end, and the Dock eould be safely moored in the Careening Hole, or Hurricane Hole, ready for constant use þÿ and if vessels required, at any time, to have their bottoms inspected, without the great trouble and expense of discharging cargo, it could be done in the Dry Dock, which would then have a great advantage over the Slip. þÿ St. Thomas Times August 3. ,
Mauifeslo of Emperor Nicola. The following important manifesto has been issued by the Emperor of Russia : þÿ " By the grace of God, we, Nicolas I., Emperor and Autocrat of all the Rus-

sians and Czar of Poland, Ac., Ac., Ac., inform till people. Be it known to our beloved and faithful subjects, the defence of our faith has always been the sacred duty of our blessed ancestors. From the day it pleased the Almighty to place me on the throne of our fathers, the maintenance of the holy obligations, with which it is inseparably connected, has been the object of our constant care and attention ; these, acting on the groundwork of the famous treaty ot Kainadjir, which subsequent solemn treaties with' tlie Ottoman Porte have fully confirmed, have ever been directed towards upholding the rights of our Church. But to our extreme grief, in latter times, notwithstanding all our efforts to defend the inviolability of the rights and privileges of our orthodox church, numerous wilful acts of the Ottoman Porte have infringed upon these rights, and threaten finally the entire overthrow of all that ancient discipline so precious to orthodoxy. All our efforts to restrain the Porte from such acts have been in vain, and even the word of the Sultan, solemnly given us by himself, was soon faithlessly broken. Having exhausted all means of conviction, and having in vain tried all the means by which our just claims could be peaceably adjusted, we have deemed it indispensable to move our armies into provinces on the Danube, in order that the Porte may see to what her stubborn ness may lead. But, even now, we have no intention of commencing war ; in occupying those provinces, we wish to

hold a sufficient pledge to guarantee for ourselves the re-establishment ot our rights under any circumstances what ever. We do not seek for conquests ; Russia does not require them. We seek to vindicate those rights which have been so openly violated. We are even vet ready to stop the movements of our armies, if the Ottoman Porte will bind itself solemnly to respect the inviolability of the orthodox church ; but if obstinacy and blindness will it otherwise, then, calling God to our aid, we leave it to Him to decide our quarrel, and in full confidence in the right hand of the Almighty, we shall move forward on behalf of the orthodox faith. " Given at Peterhoffon the 14th (26 h) day of June, in the year of the birth of Christ, 1853, and of our reign the 28th. Sealed at the Senate in St. Peterslmrgh on the 14th (26th) June, 1853. To the original of this document the own hand of his Majesty is signed. " Nikolai."

The Smyrna correspondent of the Semaphore, of Marseilles, in a letter dated the 28th ult., states that a few days previously ten Greek assassins had, hy the orders of the Austrian consul, forcibly dragged M. de Costa, a Hungarian aidede-camp of Kossuth, from his lodgings, and carried him with gre;\t violence on board the Austrian brig of war Hussar, where we was put in irons and thrown into the hold. The Hungarian and Italian refugees hearing of the outrage, applied to an American captain to interfere in the matter. After experiencing the greatest difficulty, ho had an interview with l>e Costa, whose replies, however, were not sufficiently satisfactory to induce him to interfere in his behalf. The Italian refugees in Smyrna were in the wildest state of excitement, and it was dangerous for an Austrian to be seen in the streets. Two days before the letter was despatched they had fallen upon three Austrian midshipmen, one oi whom was much bruised, and a second was pierced with daggers and killed. "The refugees have sworn to assassinate the ten Greeks employed by M. Vekbecker, and on tluir side the Greeks have sworn to kill ten Italians for every Greek that may be injured; and as the latter are the most numerous, it will be easy for them to keep their word. No arrest has yet been made, although the assassins are well known. It is said that the Italian refugees are about to be expelled. That would be justice ; but, ought not justice to fall on the author of all this mischief?" Advi-

ces from Smyrna of the 29th ult., state, that the captain of the American frigate litis laid his vessel close to the Austrian brig on board of which the Hungarian colonel, Costa, is imprisoned. The American captain has declared that he will oppose the removal of the prisoner to Trieste. The Minister of the United States claims M. de Costa, on the plea that he is a citizen of those States. The Austrian Internuncio at Constantinople has demanded that the Porte shall, within 24 hours, give him satisfaction for the outrage which the refugees at Smyrna have committed on the persons of certain officers of the Austrian navy. The London Times' correspondent gives the following further account of the affair. Martin Costa, a Hungarian refugee, and one of those exiles who accompanied Kossuth to America, had had lately returned to Smyrna, where he few been sojourning, I belive, only a days. Last Wednesday evening this man was seated in a cafe, close to the waterside, quietly smoking his narguileh, when just about sunset he found himself surrounded by an armed body of ruffians, who immediately laid hold of him. Hy a violent effort he flung two or three of these men into the water, and, finding no other means of escape, he himself sprang into the sea and swam towards a vessel, closely followed by his armed pursuers, who, quickly overtaking him, forced him, on pain of instant death, to surrender himself. He was then dragged into a boat, severely handled, and taken on board an Austrian brig-of-war

(the Husar), lying in the port, where he was heavily ironed, ft was observed that about six of his captors remained on board the Austrian brig; the rest returned on shore. On the following morning the affair became generally known, and the American Consul waited on the Consul of Austria, saying that lie understood that a native of Hungary,

3 tf ©IK © AT1S, who had become an American citizen, had been taken by force on board the Austrian man-of-war, and he wished to see the man and to ask for explanations. The Austrian Consul denied all knowledge of the fact. The American Consul then proceeded to the Austrian manof-war and requested an interview with the prisoner, which was refused ; meantime the vessel was preparing to depart. Just at that moment an American corvette, commanded by Capt. Stringham, sailed into the harbour. The consul lost no time in acquainting the captain with the affair, when they both proceeded to the Austrian Consul and demanded an interview with the prisoner. The captain of the brig was present, and he hastened on board, followed by the American captain and Consul. The prisoner was brought He was asked, " Are you an American?" on deck in irons. " Have you an American Hungarian." " No ; I am a Hungarian, and passport He answered "No; I am a I will die ?" a Hungarian." The Americans then left the vessel. Seeing, after a while, however, that the Austrian were present word to say that, " as they had on paring to depart, the American captain hoard a prisoner, carried off by force from a foreign independent territory, who had sworn allegiance to the Government of the United States, he should feel it Ins duty to insist upon the brig remaining under his guns until he received instructions from Constantinople, and that if any attempt was made to depart he would at once fire into the brig." While all this was passing between Aus-

tria and America in the harbour an immense excitement was created on shore. All the European merchants went in a body to Ali Pasha, the governor, and implored him to assert his rights and resent the violation of the Ottoman territory. The Pasha in a great fright promised to write to Constantinople for instructions. The merchants then repaired to the Casino, which and is the great reading-room, ball-room, club, and they there passed the resolution of erasing the name of every Austrian from the list of members. Hut the eventful day was doomed to end in a still more tragic scene. Towards evening, in the midst of this state of public excitement, three Austrian officers had the hardihood to go on shore and sit smoking in a cafe. They had not been long there before they were surrounded and set upon by about fifteen armed refugees, chiefly, I believe, Italians. The struggle was short ; one fell wounded by a pistol shot, the other was stabbed and jumped into the water, where he sank, and a third effected his escape in the confusion. On the following morning the body of the unfortunate and inoffensive young officer, Haron Adeberg, a young man of 18, was found, and on the same day buried. This affair has given rise to great excitement here, and to much diplomatic wrangling. The Austrian Ambassador, the Haron de Hruck, has demanded amide satisfaction of the Turkish authorities for the murder of the Austrian officer. Ali Pasha, the Governor of Smyrna, is replaced by another Pasha, late Gover-

nor of Rhodes. Several refugees have been seized, the guilty ones having, we believe, effected their escape. Meantime, Mr. Brown, the American Charge d'Affaires here, addressed a note to M. de Hruck demanding the release of Costa. The Ambassador replied, in a note betraying some temper, that he could not take such claim for a moment into consideration, since M. Costa was a Hungarian, an dittos sequent ly an of Austrian subject, amf fliat the Emperor Austria had full power over his subjects in the Ottoman territory. Mr. Brown, in return, reiterated Ins demand, sending a

copy of the oath which Costa swore to in New York, in which he swore allegiance to the Government of other States, and discarded all the United allegiance whatever, especially that of the Emperor of Austria, stating his intention to become an American citizen. Thus far the a Hair has proceeded, the Porte having dispatched Cliekib Effcndi to inquire further into it. By : i ccounts from Constantinople to the 4th we learn that Costa has provi sionally been handed over to the Austrian consul at Smyrna. Another despatch, dated Vienna, July 12, says The Costa affair is arranged. Full and entire satisfaction has been given. Severe measures will be taken against the refugees.

COMMUNICATION For the St. Croix Avis. No out can walk Company Street in the evening without having his ears tainted with the most disgusting and abominable vulgarity ; especially in the vicinity of the Week-day Market. A peaceful inhabitant living in this quarter of the town, cannot sit and enjoy a þÿmoment s sociality with a few friends, without haying his company shocked by the most immodest, obscene, and disgraceful expressions, uttered at the top of the voice in the street, by some vulgar and indecent person. The children of virtuous parents living iu this quarter of the town, while they are being | (September 2), and will be nearest to the carefinlly admonished around allured have their attention constantly the- family table, by the unseemly lewdness which is practiced and given vent to in the street. And this is not all ; but the most outrageous fights take place about this quarter, and murders might be committed, and all with impunity. 'flie shame and disgrace which these immoral practices stamp upon our community are too evident to require comment.

continue to go unnoticed by those whose province it is to punish evil-doers ? On Sunday night last, there was a desperate fight in this quarter ; and only when the venom of these disturbers of the public peace was spent, j the time ol crossing the þÿEarth path, was a little quietness restored. Not a police was to be seen in this quarter ! ! And this is invariably the case ; they are always will and then about 9 þÿo clock, you out of the way ; generally see a couple of them inarching along, and ordering peaceful individuals to quit even the very doors which they inhabit.

were to be seen in this part of the town at an early hour in the evening, much of the vagrancy I which is now committed in Company Street, and which is so disgraceful to our town, would be prevented þÿV. Christiansted, September þÿ 26th 1853. , , For llu St. Croix Avis. j It was with no little interest that I listened to the movements of Government some weeks ago, to check the awful practice of drunkenness on the Estates; by forbidding the giving of rum to the labourers. No one will question the propriety of such a step on the part of government, who is aware of ! the evil consequences of the free use of spirits among the labourers the try. But notwithstanding in the coun- þÿplanters rigidity in carrying out the injunctions laid upon them, (which is plausibly evident from the complaints of the people), yet it is equally evident that instances of drunkenness are not in the least less frequent than they were (5 months ago. Government has then entirely failed in its good attempt; and in vain will be all endeavours to check the heinous practice of intemperance, as long as Government licences the sale of spirits in the towns. Let the evil be attacked at this source, and that awful current which sweeps such destruction through our Island will be checked. Scrutator. St. Croix, 24th September 18511.

We understand that llis Majesty has been most graciously (leased, on the 18th August last, to accept the resignation of the Honorable Colonel P. de Niii.lv, Knight ol Dannebrog, from his functions as Stadshauptmand of this Island. The honorable Colonel was appointed Stadshauptmand on the 1st November 1828, and for a period of 25 years has fulfilled his duties in an efficient and soldierly manner. Order, good discipline, and harmony among was those placed under his command, the object which he always endeavored to attain, and the respect iri which he is held attests the mild manner in which he attained this purpose. Colonel df. Nully now retires from the post ol Stadshauptmand with honor, and the deep respect of this community. We understand that Major 11. M. Keutsch has been appointed Stadshauptmand.

The Scandinavian citizens of this city, of whom heretofore but little has been known, yesterday gave an annual feast, at which were entertained the officers of the Danish sloop-of-war þÿ þÿSaga, and other prominent Scandinavian citizens. The company started from the foot of Spring street, at 10 þÿo clock, yesterday morning, ,in a steamboat expressly chartered for the occasion, and reached Clermont at about half past 1 1 . The party, when assembled at the ground of the excursion, numbered about one hundred and fifty, a large portion of whom were ladies, who, according to the customs of these people, are notexcluded from entertainments of this kind. On account of the heavy rain during the morning, the party was far smaller than it would have been if the day had been fair. The invitations to the feast read that tiie excursion would be. postponed if the weather should be unfavorable, in conscience of which many were absent, taking it as a matter of course that the entertainment would be deferred. þÿDodworth ce- s lebrated brass band was engaged lor the occasion, and greatly delighted the party with their truly

8 «JN <& Hi <D 9 3L A T 9 3 artistic performances. The host at the hotel at Clermont, Mr Jones, had arranged matters with much taste and elegance , the columns of the hotel were festooned with evergreen, and the building externally was decorated with the Scandinavian flags, consisting of the Danish, Swedish and Norwegian, and with these was associated the star-spangled banner. The dinner was prepared at 4 þÿo clock in the afternoon, and the time intervening between the arrival and the dinner was spent in the ball-room in dancing and other sports upon the grounds. At 4 þÿo clock the dinner was announced, and at a table beautifully supplied, the company seated themselves, with good appetite, from all appearances, for the excellent things before them. After full, justice had been done to the eatables, the champagne began to crack and the wine to sparkle to the admiration of most present. The dinner room was decorated with the Scandinavian colors, and during the dinner and the speechifying, þÿDodworth sband sent their sweet strains from the balcony with admirable effect. As soon as the solids upon the table had been disposed of, and the liquor had taken place, its the President of the. Glee Club, Mr. Christensen, arose and addressed the guests of the occasion, the officers 9f the þÿ þÿSaga, as follows : þÿ With your permission, ladies and gentlemen, I rise to perforin a pleasant duty, which has been placed the officers of the þÿSaga, who, this day, have on me by þÿ our glee club. It is to thank

honored us with their presence. The patriotic spirit which always characterizes our national feasts displays itself this day, perhaps stronger than ever before þÿ for have we not received a greeting from our little Denmark, that blessed land we ever will bear in blessed memory, although great and praiseworthy is the new land which Providence has assigned for our present and future homes. And this greeting becomes so much more welcome, it being brought to us by men who belong to that class of þÿDenmark sons, s who, through centuries, have labored gallantly to j conferred upon their country. support the honor and the glory of our precious fatherland. In the hour of danger the Danish ; all to navy has given so striking proofs of their courage J and patriotism that their enemies themselves were forced to acknowledge and honor it. Officers of the þÿ þÿSaga, while we once beg you to receive our most heartfelt thanks for the honor you have this day shown us, and which we ever will j remember with feelings of gratitude ; we would, j j at the same time, beg you, gentlemen, when once I more you stand on þÿDenmark fertile s soil, to bring her true sons a hearty greeting from those of her TIB 8CAJ1MNAV1A1V FEAST, j sons in the mighty West, who, until their last breath, will bless the memory of that spot where first they lisped a þÿmother name, s and tasted the joys of innocence and youth. Ladies and gentlemen, I give you The corvette þÿSaga, and our guests hergal- þÿ lr.nt officers.

Nine cheers were then given, when, Lieut. W. Mariboo, on the part, of the officers of the þÿ þÿSaga, replied as follows, in the Danish language Ladies and gentlemen. þÿ As one of the officers . of the þÿ þÿSaga, I rise to offer you my most sincere thanks, on the part of myself and my brother officers, for the honor you have shown us. I regret that some one else has not been called upon to perform the pleasing task of responding to the toast, just proposed, in honor of my associates. It is a cheering feeling for every Dane to know that whenever he comes to a foreign land, and meets a countryman, he at the same time, meets a brother, in the true sense of the word. (Applause.) The truth and the proof of this has manifested itself more strikingly than I could have hoped for, by the reception which we officers have met with on this occasion. I am not prepared, gentlemen, to express my feelings at this time, in so full a manner as I desire But, gen-

tlemen, let me only wish that you may prosper, whether you will seek your happiness here, or in your own country. But this I am sure of, if you select the first, you will always remain faithful to your own Denmark, the land of your fathers and if you select the second, I doubt not that you will be as true in your adopted as in your native land. I give you þÿ All honor and success to the Scandinavians of North þÿAmerica.

The largest Tree in the world. There is a cedar-tree growing in the mountains of Calaveras Country, California, about twenty miles north-east of þÿMurphy s which is said to be the largest in the world. A correspondent of the Sonora Herabl, who recently made an excursion to see it, thus describes it: þÿ þÿ At the ground, its circumference was 92 feet ; four feet above that it was 88; and ten feet above that it was GI feet in circumference ; and after that the tapering of the shaft was very gradual. Its height, as measured by Captain H., is 300 feet ; but we made it but 285. This tree is by no means a deformity, as most trees with large trunks are. It is throughout one of perfect symmetry, while its enormous proportions inspire the beholder with emotions of awe and sublimity. Elegance and beauty are inseparable concomitants of ils grandeur. I have said that this is the largest tree yet discovered in the world. It is so. The celebrated tree of Freemont would have | prising owner and builder of to grow many centuries before it could pretend to be anything but a young brother. It is said that a tree was once found in Senegal, in Africa, whose trunk measured 90 feet in þÿcircumference.

VALUE or EXPERIENCE in AUSTRALIA A correspondent of the Builder writes: þÿ þÿ You will, doubtless, ere this, have heard of my being at the diggings, and of my having returned unsuccessful, inasmuch as I got very little gold, but I got experience, which is sometimes even more valuable. I did not stay long, just enough to spend my money, all and then returned to town fit for any sort of work, the second best state that a man

can be m when arriving here. I give the preference to the capitalist, but the workman is next best, and in application of my newly-acquired ability 1 took a job to work granite at 27s. per day, the first that presented itself. This job served me till I got a few acquaintances, and a little knowledge of the place, which did not take me more than three weeks, before I had my flrst job, and since then I have gone on gradually increasing every week. I have just now two Government jobs, small ones, and I do the work of the Melbourne Water Company. 1 have likewise going on a large stone building for one of our principal timber merchants, and a few other small ones, and 1 expect soon to have the order to commence the Melbourne and þÿHobson s Bay Railway, having obtained the lirst contract on that line. I said to you before leaving that l was tired of being a foreman. I am glad I arrived at this conclusion. Allow me to observe here that there is no fear of going on upon a false footing in this place, for credit is almost unknown ; accounts only remain for a week, when they must be paid in cash ; wages the same, so that, if a man can get along for that time, there is no fear for the future. Our work must be done and paid for before we draw our cash, so that there can be no þÿ in this town. I And a considerable difficulty in going a head at present, but, as every job leaves a sur plus, l hope soon to be without trouble or expediency in business. Our greatest difficulties in business are those un-

known in England, that is, to get men and þÿmaterials. A second letter from the same writer, dated June 8, says : þÿ þÿ This business has increased astonish ingly. He now has a quarry of his own is entering more generally into the build ing business; has a C.E. for a clerk; the late station-master at þÿKing s-cross, who gave up a good situation to go there, is carting stones for him, the station-master having got two horses and carts ; and several other late employers on the Great Northern are mentioned as at work for him. lie says the place is quite like þÿKing s-cross, and it is difficult to believe that l am on the other side of the þÿglobe.

AUSTRIA. The Sietle has the following remarks on the memorandum of the Austrian Government to the Courts of Europe with reference i a friendly to the affair of Kossta, who was claimed b\ the American Consul: þÿ þÿ The principles set forth in this memorandum are true, but who is it that has violated them ? Evidently Austria, which in a neutral port caused to be arrested, in a most offen- j give manner, a man placed under the protection of the flag of the United States. If the I legality of M Kossia's naturalisation, he was Austrian Consul had any doubt as to the bound to apply to the officer in the command of the American station, and to ask him to oppose the escape of that refugee until the point of law had been properly cleared up. 1 Austria, disdaining the use of legal proceedings, attempted to obtain justice for herself by force. And now she complains of having met witli a legitimate opposition to her acts of violence! We do not entertain the slightest doubt that the American corvette, St. Louis, would, without a moment's hesitation have opened fire on the Hussar brig, if the captain of that Austrian vessel had refused to give up M. Kossta into the hands of the i French Consul until the question of nationality should have been decided. Kossta had not fulfilled one of the conditions essential to obtain naturalisation in the United States þÿ namely, five years' of consecutive residence on the territory of the Union. But M. Koss a was admitted to swear fidelity to the

American Government, and he received an American passport. It was on the faith of j that passport that he proceeded to Turkey in Asia, and it is allowable to declare that the affair does not concern him any more ; it lies between the Government of the Union and every Government which undertakes to violate the guarantee given by the United States to M. Kossta. Austria has taken good care not to place the dispute on that ground. In the hope of bringing over to her side France, who has always sustained the cause of neutrals, the Cabinet of Vienna has indulged in the lucubration which it has lately published, and which, of itself, condemns the Austrian Consul ; for, once more, if the right of neutrals has been violated, it was bv that functionary who seized on Kossta. without applying to the American Commodore, and without deigning to take the opinion of the authorities of Smyrna. Turkey, always accustomed to yield to a protection which does not protect her, has dismissed Ali Pasha, the Governor of Smyrna, formerly Grand Vizier, and one of the most intelligent men of the Ottoman Empire There is no danger that the same treatment will fall on the American captain. The United States will uphold the respect due to their flag, and, rather than abandon a man protected by an American passport, they would burn down Trieste, and again raise up the Republic of Venice. They care little about the treaties of 1815, before which the Governments of Europe stop short, because these treaties were the affair of prin-

ces at the expense of the rights of nations. In truth, when all slumbers in a kind of fetichism for the status quo, it would be almost to be wished that Austria would venture to blave the anger of the United States. But she will not attempt it, well knowing that the Americans would not hesitate to defend the right as it requires to be defended. However, we enregister. as of good augury, the

ST. 0 3t t> 2 X A?J8. memorandum of Austria, for it is of a nature to remove all hesitation on the part of the Government of General Pierce to stretch out hand to those persons who suffer in Europe from the pretensions and acts of Austrian þÿdespotism. þÿ The Observer.

We learn from pretty fair authority that another attempt had been made to set fire to Road Town, Tortola, but fortunately it was discovered before the (lames took possession of the building where the vde incendiary had set his lighted torch þÿ otherwise that unfortunate little country may have been another mass of ruins. The offender has not been traced; and þÿ tis no strange thing now, we are told, to rise in the morning and find several horses and other animals lying dead about. þÿ having been stabbed by the þÿassassin knife s on the previous night. It is also stated by our informant that the Governor-General was about issuing a Commission to institute a Special Court for the purpose of trying the Rebels. Privy Councils were being held daily ; Government had advertised for tenders for thoroughly repairing the Poor House, in order to convert the same into a Military liarrack for the Troops.

MONTSERRAT : The Antigua Observer furnishes the subjoined melancholy particulars of the ravages of Yellow Fever at Montserrat : þÿ Yellow Fever, we regret exceedingly to state, prevails to a distressing extent in the sister Colony of Montserrat. þÿ On Saturday last, an express vessel arrived here with a Despatch from the late President þÿBooth Lady, s requesting the aid of a Medical Gentleman. At the instance, we believe, of His Excellency the Governor, our talented young practitioner, Dr. Adam Nicholson, proceeded to Montserrat in the evening, and upon his arrival found the President in a state of collapse. His Honor, we lament to say, expired on the afternoon of Sunday, the 21st instant, in the 59th year of his age. The decease of Captain Booth has caused universal sorrow to the Community over which he presided. His liberal principles, and entire exemption f rom Colonial prejudices, justly endeared him to all classes of the Inhabitants. þÿ Another victim was Dr. Claude McKechnie, a gentleman well known and highly esteemed in this island, whose untimely death is deeply regretted, not only at Montserrat, but also by his numerous friends in this island. þÿ Several other deaths had occurred from this fatal malady, and the Community is quite panic stricken. Dr. Nicholson has been prevailed upon to remain at Montserrat, to his great inconvenience, until some other Medical Gentleman may be procured from this, or one of the neighbouring Islands. þÿ The Widow of the lamented Presi-
dent, who labours under the Epidemic, arrived here this morning.
