Weekly Record

The inhabitants of Cumana, tired of supporting the scandalous administration of General Jose Gregorio Monagas, and impelled by the heroic sentiments of patriotism, declared on the 4th June, the disacknowledgment of his government, and proclaimed the Federative system, as the most useful to the rights of its children. From that day the people of Cumana entertained no other idea than that of supporting, in a worthy manner, the contest in which the rulers of Venezuela were preparing to involve them; and, confident in the sacredness of that cause which they maintained, and in their acknowledged bravery, proudly considered themselves already masters of victory, awaiting with enthusiasm the commencement of the struggle which their enemies rashly threatened. Forty-live days had elapsed, since that declaration. It was on the 15th of July ; the sun, with all the splendour and brilliancy which is so often seen during the beautiful days of a trophical sky, shed its rays, and by its attractive appearance seemed to be the harbinger of happy events; and a mild and refreshing breeze sweetly tempered the sultriness or heat of the noon-day hour. Nature arrayed in all her beauties, seemed to desire to smile with splendour for a last lime , on the inhabitants of Cumana, and on that very day in which numbers were to be buried under its ruins ! There was nothing to forebode that a terrible disaster was about to fall on that remarkable land þÿ perhaps the loveliest of Venezuela: no presentiment existed in the breast of

any one of the approach of a great misfortune, lulled as they were, by that enthusiasm which had never been greater among the inhabitants; nor was there any physical symptoms in the aspect of nature, which seldom shewed itself more placid or composed than at that eventful period. It was at 25 minutes past 2, p. m. ; the steady breeze which prevailed during the day, on a sudden ceased, and the wind shifted to the West, blowing severely. At the moment of this extraordinary change in the atmosphere, a severe commotion was felt ; the earth shook under our teet, and the buildings

continued trembling on their foundations. It was at first supposed that this phenomenon would prove similar to the Earthquakes which have been of frequent occurrence in Cumana : but, at the end of a few seconds, the moderate oscillation was succeeded by a terrible shock, as if the foundation of the earth had been broken ; so that no one could retain their position, but were shaken to and fro by an irresistible power. Amidst the violent rumbling caused by the catastrophe and noise þÿ the shrieks of distress and despair from the victims burst from the ruins, and the cry of mercy from the inhabitants! but that appeal was in vain ; it was too late, inasmuch that the fate of the city was sealed þÿ the destruction of Cumana already accomplished ! A thick cloud of dust immediately covered the atmosphere for a few moments ; and on being dispersed, the whole city appeared to the sight in ruins ! The inhabitants who had escaped, by rushing to the public squares and streets, assembled in groups ; many covered with dust and blood, and in their appearance, exhibiting all the excitement of the greatest terror or despair ; whilst from the ruins conld be distinctly heard the cries and groans of the victims þÿ the wounded and dying, yielding their last sigh ! Language would fail to describe, with all the strength of reality, the calamity which has taken place in Cumana: the greatest scope of imagination would, with difficulty, pourtray the extent of a disaster so terrible ! The earth remains

in chasms and fissures in innumerable places. The sea retired from its bed a few yards at the commencement of the catastrophe, and as if to recover its strength to return afterwards, with extraordinary impetus, and to penetrate more thjn one hundred yards into the city. A few springs suddenly presented themselves, and the waters of the Manzanaus, which runs through the town, rose, at the moment, several feet. None of the public edifices in the city remain standing ! The four Temples which it contained as well as the two Chapels ; the quarters of the infantry ; the Hospital of Charity ; that of the Lepers ; the Bridge ; the Fort of San Antonio, the Colliseuin, although not completed ; þÿ all have been totally destroyed. Many private houses have crumbled down on their foundations ; others are thrown in a leaning position, threatening to fall at every moment, others arc so shattered and considerably injured, as to be insecure and untenantable. The number of victims cannot yet be ascertained ; but it is supposed that it will not be less than 500 ! There is not eme family, vho has not some loss to lament. Among the remarkable victims of this lamentable catastrophe, it is necessary to mention, especially, the name of Colonel Ramon Perez, the Military Chief of the Province. Venezuela will mourn the melancholy loss of a Citizen so distinguished for his zealous patriotism, and so esteemed for the nobleness of heart, and the amiability of his character. Pure and virtuous, as well as a

pattern of probity ; after having been for a period of thirty years in the discharge of public affairs of the highest importance ; he leaves a numerous family in the greatest distress and desolation, with only a name, which, history will record as worthy of occupying a place alongside of our most eminent Patriots ! The value of the property destroyed will amount to several millions of dollars: it is sufficient to state, that Cumana has ceased to exist ! The buildings having been erected with a particular regard to avoid the disasters of earthquakes, proved the means of allowing the principal portion of the inhabitants sufficient time to effect their escape. BY AN EYE WITNESS.

The Returned Californian; OR DISCONTENT CL' RED. þÿ What is the use of toiling unremittingly, year after year, to acquire a bare competence, when one successful year at the mines of California has enriched for life such a man as Gilbert þÿDanvers? These words were spoken by a worthy and prosperous citizen of Boston to his wife, in bitterness of spirit, as he neat, moodily Hung himself on the sofa arran- comfortable, and tastefully in his ged parlour. The speaker had but just returned, with his amiable partner, from a visit to one of the successful seekers of gold in California soil. The man had owed him a debt of no very great magnitude it is true, but an amount worth receiving. The ladies of the respective parties had been slightly acquainted, and as report spoke loudly of the marvellous change of circumstances which had so suddenly occurred, Mrs. Wakefield had accompanied her spouse to one of those delightful towns within a few þÿminutes ride (per rails) of this favored city. The money due was promptly paid, and this most important part of the visit satisfactorily accomplished þÿ yet strange, it seemed, that Mr. Wakefield returned with the air of a disappointed man. This is the solicitous eye of affection noticed during the transit the in the cars, was reaching home, mystery and, on explained by the peevish ejaculation of momentary discontent with which we have introduced the gentleman to the þÿreaders notice. þÿ Oh, my husband, it could not be that you are repining at the success of Gilbert Danvers, or envy the gaudy display

we have just witnessed in the family? They have handsomer furniture than we can boast, more showy and more modem, it is true þÿ but ours is good enough to satisfy us, under the knowledge that it has been honourably earned and honestly paid for. I am sure it would have been a sore trial to all of us had you been absent for two whole years, and exposed to the hardships, sickness, dangers and temptations, of the golden land ! I am thankful it was not þÿso. þÿ You are very kind and consoling, dearest, but only the more do I regret that my means are not equal to my wishes, for your sake. Had þÿ 1 but the riches to reward you, and Heed it not, we are comfortable, nay, we are happy, if you but will it so. Now do not deem me envious or uncharitable, and I will say, I really fear that something wrong lurks beneath þÿ seeming of the Danvers some hidden the specious cause which embitters the gilded change ! Marked you not the restless wandering

3 T SI A T J 3. of the eye, the nervous manner of our host, as you commented on his good luck ? þÿ No, þÿindeed, replied Mr. Wakefield. < I only thought of the change so short a period had made in our situations. When I saw him last, previous to his embarkation, he was a penniless adventurer, leaving behind him an impoverished family and heavy debts. 1 then felt pity, and never would have pressed for payment under such circumstances. Now what a contrast! He is elevated to a pitch of luxury which I cannot hope in years of plodding industry to obtain ! I cannot afford you such rich dresses, such splendid jewellery, as are lavishly presented to Mrs. Danvers. Can I indulge my wife and family (however dear to me), with a trip to Europe? The lady replied : þÿ Be yourself again, husband mine, never never have 1 known you thus give way to such discontent. Think not that I shall pine for such extravagance as l have this day heard boasted of. We are amply provided, and you are with us to share the happiness of which you are the þÿcentre. þÿ Oh ! Marianne, who could resist such arguments þÿ! said the husband, brightening up. þÿ Well, surely I hope to prevail þÿ! replied the lady with a winning smile, þÿ and you may depend upon it, if our success in life be slow, it is but the more assured, and even the more valuable, because we can estimate the value of money better than those to whom it comes suddenly and almost without measure. Besides, from the novelty of the thing, and its present seeming su-

perabundance, 1 should not wonder that these very people, from the rate at which they are now living, would come to the end of their funds as speedily as they were attained þÿ and then how will they be situated? Worse than before, assuredly, for they will be despised and ridiculed into the bargain þÿ! This is very true, þÿcertainly, replied Mr. Wakefield, languidly, þÿ but I have been bilious the last few days, and this must excuse the acrimony of my feelþÿings! 1 You have fatigued yourself too much in your unceasing care to provide your family with the elegancies as well as the decencies of' city life but you must not þÿ be too anxious for the superfluities of this world, on our account, lest life itselfþÿ your own life so valuable to us all þÿ should pay the price þÿ! This was said so kindly and sincerely, that the transient spirit ot repining fled before the cheering voice of affection. The merchant returned to his desk the next day, contented to plod slowly along the hackneyed path to a moderate fortune : þÿ and the extraordinary good luck of Danvers was not allowed to weigh on his thoughts. The reasonable remarks of his wife restored his usual complacency and content. A few months rolled away, changing in their course the fortunes of many an anxious mortal þÿ but ere the year closed, the envied possessor of the sudden fortune was an exile from home, family and country. He had been reduced to an ignominious flight to save himself from a prosecution !

Humour, for once, did not magnify the amount of wealth attributed to Mr. Danvers þÿ nor were the surmises of people, as to his honesty, unfounded or incorrect. þÿ How infatuated, as well as unprincipled, must the misguided man have been to think that he could appropriate to his own use the money entrusted to his care, without being called to account for it? So spake Mr. Wakefield to his lady, in reference to Mr. Danvers. þÿ Pray let me know what has come out about þÿhim, said she, þÿ I have not heard the full þÿparticulars. 1 Much about the same as you formerly predicted. Danvers has cleared out. The money was almost expended. He is branded with guilt, and the family is disgraced and þÿhumbled. þÿ Indeed ! What had he done? How he obtained the gold þÿ? þÿ It turns out that Mr. Danvers, during his siiort stay, accumulated a merely moderate amount of dust, and becoming impatient to leave a spot where numbers were dearly paying for the glittering ore, by sickness and death, he took passage to return to his native State. 4 The day previous to sailing, an acquaintance, who had been two years at the mines, and uniformly successful in his labors, and had proposed coming home by the same opportunity, was suddenly cut down by sickness, and being utterly prostrate, he could not lie moved. It was useless to flunk of his quitting California in such a state, indeed little hopes were entertained that he could survive the malignant attack. In this emergency the mind of the sick man,

whose name was Roberts, was greatly agitated by fears that in case of his death his hoarded stock of gold-dust þÿ for which he had bartered health and comfort þÿ might fall into the hands of the vultures who surrounded him, and thus his family never be benefitted by his toil and suffering. 1 The sick man murmured his griel and fears before the friend who was about to depart for that Boston, which lie felt as if doomed never again to behold, and Danvers offered to take charge of the precious deposit, promising personally to deliver it into the appointed hands. 4 Rejoiced at the opportunity of providing for his family in case of his demise, Roberts said that if he die he must, death would indeed lie robbed of its chief terror, when lie had an assurance that his treasure would reach those for whom he had worked and endured. 44 Such was the extreme debility and apparent hopeless state of the sick man, that the fatal temptation to sin arose in the mind of Danvers. 4 Who is to know' þÿ doubtless thought he þÿ 4 that the gold dust I have thus received is not a part of mine own honest gain ? What worse of all will the rightful owner be, should 1 keep the deposit, than if it had been ' consumed by the sharpers of < !alifo(nia ?

þÿ Woful delusion ! Yet such suggestions of the devil prevailed. The result vve know. He kept the money and used it as his own. He lived high, cut a dash, and dazzled the eyes of many, who wondered how so much money could be made in so short a time. You smile, my þÿdear, said Mr. Wakefield, þÿ and well you may, for I have not forgotten our visit, or the ensuing converþÿsation. þÿ But you have not told me how Danvers was unmasked, and what brought about the þÿcatastrophe. þÿ That is soon done. The supposed dying man, when relieved from the oppressive anxiety for the safety of his precious earnings, recovered, and wrote home to his family a few lines, which gave rise to the floating reports regarding Danvers, but the allusions were too vague to be acted on by them. Nothing could be proved. The reply which Mr. Roberts received 1 from his wife satisfied him that the money or its equivalent, had not reached its destination, and he wrote back, stating the particulars, but enjoining silence, as he would return to Boston the very instant his health would permit, in hopes of confronting his false friends in time to recover a part of the þÿgold. However, an unguarded speech made before a child, reached the ears of Danvers in time to enable him to decamp. He learned enough to know that daily the return was expected of that man whom, of a trusty friend, he had treacherously made a deluded victim. þÿ 1 am told that he quitted the city that same night, with but a scanty sum

in his purse, and set out to seek some unknown spot wherein to hide his guilt and shame. He is now bankrupt alike in honor, credit, money and þÿhappiness. þÿ How is it with the unfortunate family? enquired Mrs. Wakefield, emphatically feeling for their desolation. þÿ His wife gave herself such airs during the short season of their grandeur, that I fancy few pity her, and the children are too young to understand or feel the change. She will have to return with mortification to her former way of providing for herself, I þÿexpect. þÿ It must be a sad reverse. Nevertheless this short career and its attendant circumstances may warn people not to be in too great a hurry to get rich, said Mrs. Wakefield ; þÿ and let us profit by it, to enjoy the blessings which surround us at home and be contented with our city þÿ lot and domestic þÿenjoyments. Dearest wife, I am cured ! I am content ! Nothing shall lure me from the bosom of my family to the fatal Eldorado þÿ I shall not soon forget the story of the Returned þÿCalifornian.

THE CHOLERA. The returns from the Continent still continue to give accounts ot the rapid spread of the disease both cast, west, north, and south. In Norway it is making great ravages, although not to so great an extent as it did in Denmark. In Stockholm, Istad, Carberona, and Goturnberg, the pestilence lias been very fatal, in many places the deaths already being 3 per cent, of the entire population. This is very great, especially when it is considered that the disease rarely attacks any hut those above 15 years of age ; if, therefore, the adult population is only taken, the proportion of deaths to population would be much higher. In Copenhagen the the disease seems to have worn itself out, deaths at present not being more than two or

three a day. It has, in fact, attacked I almost all that were in any way susceptible, and having carried þÿoft its victims it has proceeded to the provinces, where it is now quite as fatal as it was in the capital city. In Jutland it is especially raging. To give some idea of the frightful manner in which Copenhagen has been decimated, it will suffice to show what is the difference between the mortality in that city during the present summer, and what it was in the metro- ! polis in 1848 and 1849. In the metropolis the total deaths in 1848-49 were 14,610, or at the rate of 62 in 10,000 persons living. In Copenhagen the deaths during the summer have been 4,015, or at the rate of 277 in 10,000 living, so that if the cholera had been as fatal in London as in Copenhagen, the deaths instead of having been 14,610, would have been 65,417, or more than the deaths in all England. This is enough to make the public very anxious, for as it has become epidemic in this country, we cannot hope that the deaths will be in the same ratio as before. We are the more inclined to this opinion, from the fact that whenever the disease has made its appearance this summer it has assumed a much more malignant form than heretofore, and we see no such difference either in the habits, constitution, or mode of living of our continental neighbours, as to lead us to anticipate a more favourable result. The boldest of all reformers is the man who undertakes to alter the pursuits and employments, the habits and thoughts, of the common people. The good of a change is generally remote and prospective ; its evil is present, immediate, and tangible. The first may strike the mind of the statesman or the philosopher ; the second comes home to the feelings of the multitude. þÿ Give us back the ten days you have robbed us of, you þÿrascal, was the salutation with which the mob greeted one of those most active in introducing the new style of chronological reckoning into England. The

3 (Q people really believed themselves aggrieved, and it was of little use to tell them of the Gregorian calendar and point out the errors involved in the pbpular calculation. The mob reasoned then as the Greek Church reasons now ; the wrong mode of reckoning was what they were used to, and they hated accordingly the man who broke through an established custom, though it were for their benefit. There is one advantage in the spread of education, and that is that it renders these changes easier, first, by teaching men to reason, and thus emancipating them from the dominion of prejudice, and, secondly, by enabling them more easily to understand and conquer the difficulties of the alteration. þÿ London Times.

Oclira Slump. A new and most valuable article of commerce is likely to be added to the resources of Louisiana, in the Hemp made from the Ochra plant. We have a specimen of it before us, the threads of which are ten feet in length. We have seen cording made from it, equal in strength and appearance to any we have ever seen manufactured from the ordinary hemp. We cannot say how rope made of ochra, would answer for marine purposes, but, whether if it would or not, pal sufferers. As was expected, the I there are so many purposes for which it can be employed, that its value would not be depreciated any great to extent were it unfit for application in this particular. Bagging of every description, used in commerce for packing, can be manufactured of it, better than with the common hemp þÿ for, besides being equal in strength, it possesses one great advantage over the other þÿ it will lie in water for three years and it will not rot. Door mats and floor matting can be manufactured of it, and it takes dye splendidly, matting can be made as varied as carpets. No machinery has been employed to dress any of the specimens we have seen, pressed by The Times , is no more than j and it looks as clean as any operation could well make it. Hemp, we believe is worth about 100 dollars per ton. The ochra hemp can be prepared for market and sold for only half that price. A company of gentlemen in connection with the proprietors of the City Hotel, we believe, are about to invest some capital and enterprise in the cultivation

and manufacture of this hemp. They are greatly encouraged in this enterprise by the opinion of some of the most scientific men in the country in relation to its certain success. The expense of manufacturing this hemp for the market will be inconsiderable. The refuse wood from the stems of the ochra will more than suffice to supply fuel tor the steam engine. The tow is admirably adapted for mattresses, and is superior to moss for bedding. The upholsters are already on the qui vivc to obtain it. VVe are collecting some information in relation to this business, and shall, with all despatch lay it before our readers. þÿ New Orleans Delta.

From the Grenada Weekly Record, September 15, 1853. Amongst the Parliamentary Proceedings communicated to us by the papers received per last mail, we are glad to perceive that the subject ol' the emigration from China to the West Indies had come under the consideration of the Commons, with a view to facilitate such emigration by a reduction of the superficial space computed to be allowed to ihe emigrants. The Times of the 15th ultimo, informs us as follows: þÿ " Onthe 13th, ihe House went into committee on the þÿPassenger s Act Amendment Hill, when, in reply to a question from Sir II. Willoughby, on the object of the Bill, Mr. Peei. stated that its object was to correct some anomalies in the present law, and to facilitate emigration from China to the West Indies. The West India Colonies and Guiana desired to have labour imported from China. Not only had there been great mortality in vessels which had gone from Amoy to British Guiana and other colonies, bat speculators had employed Chinese crimps, who had practised deception on their fellow-countrymen. If the emigration were to continue, it was indispensable that it should continue under Government control, with a Government agent, and from a Government part. No native would be allowed to embark on any vessel without its being ascertained where he was going to, and without his entering into a contract. But, unfortunately, the þÿPassengers Act, though it applied to Hongkong, did not apply to other ports in China, as no others were in British possession. The þÿPassenger Act s required that 15 super-

ficial feet should be allowed in vessels for each emigrant; and the object of the present bill was to empower the governors of British colonial possessions to reduce that allowance to 12 feet, which, it was thought, might safely be done in the case of Asiatics. The only question was, whether real injury would be done to the health of the Chinese if the space were reduced. There was every reason to believe that the reduction might be made without injury. There had long existed an extensive emigration to the Mauritius from the East Indies. In 1850 and the three seasons which had since elapsed no fewer than 8,000 Coolies had been sent to the Mauritius. The þÿPassengers Act did not apply to that emigration, which was regulated by enactments of the Indian Government. The allowance for each passenger was 12 feet, and there was no reason to believe that Asiatics from China would require more space than those was from India. The þÿPassengers Act intended to apply to the emigration of Europeans to Australia and New Zealand. The expense of transport was greatly increased by granting a space of 15 superficial feet to Chinese passing to that West Indies, and he apprehended the if the power were not given to reduce the space, that emigration would go from Chinese ports without the Government having that control which it was desirable they should have. þÿ The bill then passed through comþÿmittee.

The French Islands. The French Colonists are bestirring themselves in a manner well worthy of themselves, and of the critical situation in which they have been placed by the sudden emancipation of their slaves. In addition to the efforts made by the ladies of Guadeloupe, through the agency of Madame ltiby, we learn that the Commercial Firm of Ch. Chevalier, of Nantes, are under engagement for the importation of African Immigrants upon a large scale, into the French Islands. It would also appear that an offer has been made to the French Planters, by one of the first houses in London, to procure them a supply of labourers from Madeira. Upon these several schemes and their practicability as regards Martinique, the Editor of La France d' Outre-Mer has some excellent remarks ; and he adverts with peculiar satisfaction to the moderate terms proposed to our own Legislature by Captain McLean. Another important advantage of the French Islands, and of which they are justly proud, is the steam communication established among them for local purposes. The St. Ficrre and St. Louis have been for some time in active employment, and a third steamer, called the Madinina, recently built at Nantes, is soon expected out. We also find mention of an Insurance Company about to be established in Paris, with the title of L'Egide dc la Province, chielly with a view to colonial operations. þÿ St. Lucia Palladium, September 17. :ior Facts and Scraps.

The « AVIS." G/irittiansted, Tuesday the '2bth October 1853. The Hurricane-Season, which terminates to-day, has been a favorable one; for we have been providentially spared the dangers and son. Bolts, bars, of this perilous sea- other fastenings have not been required ; and we can safely lay them by for the with island has been blessed present. The good weather þÿ fine rains with alternate sunshine. Vegetation is in a prosperous and beautiful condition þÿ the canes are nearly all ripe, which happy the certainly fill the hearts of result must planters with delight ; having fair prospects of ail early and abundant crop, if sufficient manual labor can only be procured to take it oil". The people of thj? towns have an opportunity to-day, in visiting the different places of worship, to express their heartfelt thanks to the Giver of All- Good, for the many favors lie has so bountifully showered down upon us. The country people, we regret however to say, have not this advantage; as the day is not a general holiday. We, therefore, entertain the hope that this Pseudo-Holiday will be transformed next year into a real one.

The Mails, per European Packet, arrived here on Friday last. The accounts from Eastern Europe are very unfavorable. Russia yet occupies the Turkish provinces of Moldavia and Wallachia. The united French and English fleets have entered the Dardanelles. It is said that a remonstrance to the Sultan, has emanated lrom the Ulemas, proposing to His Majesty either to abdicate or go to war. It is, however, expected that the advice of experienced counsellors, and

the remonstrances of the Western Powers, may yet be able to save Europe from the consequences of the stubbornness of the Czar, and the imbecility of the Sultan. The Cholera was raging to a fearful extent both'in Newcastle and in Gateshead. The number of deaths at Newcastle, from 31st Augt. to 23d Septbr. amounted to 1,056. At Gateshead up to 23d September, 329.

The following important intelligence has just been made public by a cotemporary generally well informed on the subject of foreign affairs, and particularly so on the Turkish question (the Morning Post). If the information which it conveys should prove correct, then " war" is inevitable, or Russia will be disgraced for ever in the eyes of Europe : þÿ "The latest intelligence from Constantinople is of an alarming character. The popular excitement had reached a high pitch, and although there is no confirmation of the details reported by a private telegraph, a source of information which has often proved erroneous, nevertheless we have reason to believe that the state of affairs was, at the latest dates, so menacing, that the English and French Ambassadors had used the discretion vested in them, and had required six men-of-war, three English and three French, to pass the Dardanelles. "Accordingly on the I4th or 15th inst., the ships in question had anchored in the Sea of Marmora." » This important step was necessary on every account, and especially to give a strong moral support to the Sultan, who needs such aid, as well as against internal fanaticism, as against external aggression. The latest news informs

us that there was a complete schism in the Turkish Cabinet, one part of which was but too much disposed to listen to passion rather than to reason. If such a party were in the ascendant, then might we look for a revolution at Constantinople, leading directly to a state of anarchy, in which the life of no Christian, of whatever country, would be safe. It is well on every account that the fleets have passed the Dardanelles. By this time the whole force has followed the six men-of-war, which were but the vanguard, and at the moment at which we write we may assure the public that the combined fleets, under the command of Admiral Dundas and Hamelin, are riding at anchor in the Sea of Marmora. And why should they not? The treaty of 1841 is not at this moment in existence. Treaties are abrogated by war, and who will pretend that war has not commenced? The treaty of 1841 stipulates that no vessels of war shall pass " the Dardanelles so long as the Porte is at peace." The Porte, however, being no longer at peace, our fleets have per- a fect right to enter the Sea of Marmora. All juris-consults, without exception, agree in recognising the fact that, when the territory of one state is invaded by another state by force of arms, such invasion is an act of war ; and that, when it is committed without reasonable cause, it is an act of piracy. " Nothing can be clearer than the Treaty of Adrianople, between Russia and Turkey 'The Pruth shall hence- þÿ forward he the frontier of the two em-

pires.' The Russians, however, have crossed the Pruth in arms, for the avowed purpose of extorting by force that to which they have no shadow of right, recognised either by Turkey or by Europe. The prodigious armaments of Turkey show how plainly she considers the deed of Russia as an act of war, and as such it has hcen recognised publicly by our own Ministers and by the whole of Europe. "The passage of the Dardanelles, which has just taken place, is, therefore, completely justifiable by all maxims of ! (Translated from the Spanish , for " The international law, by the special proviof our ally. sions of treaties, and by the necessities . _ " If this step lias not been taken before, it has been because it was almost impossible to believe that a power such as Russia, pretending to such high principle, could really intend to persist a in shameless and unjustifiable act of piracy, and it was wished rather to construct a bridge for her escape from an awkward and mistaken position, than to provoke her pride by bluntly acting as mere justice would have required. " The step is, however, now taken, and cannot be retraced so long as the dispatch in which Russia re-asserts her first pretensions remains uncancelled. I he fleets will not quit the Bosphorous and the Sea of Marmora until the Russians have re-crossed the Pruth. If, at the latest hour, Russia he ready to acknowledge her folly, and negotiate upon air terms, renouncing the impossible

ST, ATI 3 pretensions 'she has put forward against Turkey, peace may be yet secured. The fleets in the Bosphorous occupy a position which balances that of the Russians in the Principalities; and now, if Count Nesselrode choose to ask tor simultaneous evacuation, his proposal might be entertained ; whereas, when the fleets were only at Besika, the requirement was absurd. " The period of negotiation, then, is closed, unless a return to that mode of settlement be procured by retractation on the part of Russia þÿ a course which is yet open to her. Failing such retractation, we must expect to hear that discussion has been superseded by action."

Russian Poisoner. þÿ A Paris paper the ( Constitutionnel ) states the following circumstance: þÿ "A European physician, who arrived some months back at Constantinople, obtained by dint of solicitation the direction of the military hospital at Schumala. It appears that Oilier Pasha soon perceived that this person kept up mysterious relations with Russian spies, and in consequence he kept on his guard. Soon after, being warned that there was an intention to poison him, he feigned to be indisposed, and sent for the medical man in question to attend him. This person, after examining the patient, went out to prepare a calming potion, which, on his return, he presented to Omer Pasha to drink. The General-in-Chief of the Turkish army requested the physician to taste it first l himself, and, as the other refused to do so, he forced him to drink the whole of it in his presence. Seeing that the physician then wanted to hurry out, he forced him to remain in the tent, in order that he might judge of the effect of the poison." He died in a few hours.

Weekly Record ."> JOSE GREGOIllO MONACAS, <$-c , <K considering, 1st þÿ That the brilliant triumphs obtained by the constitutional forces over the rebels who took up arms, in the Republic, have defeated the designs of the sworn enemies of the liberty of Venezuela, re-established the empire of the constitution and of the Laws, and proved the powerful opinion which con tributes to the sapport of the National Government : þÿ 2nd þÿ That under present circumstances, the public peace and the repose of society demands a general measure to discontinue as soon as possible, all prosecutions and their results, to restore the tranquility of the public mind, and general confidence : þÿ 3rd þÿ That the Executive Power, respecting as is its duty, the vindication of the Laws, and the many sacrifices which have been made by the Nation to protect the Country, ought to exhibit the national clemency, as far as it is compatible with public security, and with

the protection required for the consolidation of its institutions, its prosperity, and the common weal of the people : þÿ By virtue of the power which I am invested by the 4th Section and 118th Article of the Constitution, and in conformity with the Council of Government, 1 DECREE, Article 1. þÿ Are suspended all prosecutions and all ordinary penalties of the law entered into or pronounced against all the individuals who have appertained, or, in whatsoever manner, been found implicated with the rebels who took up arms in the present year in the Provinces of Aragua, Carabobo, Cuarico, Margaritta, Cumana, and Barcelona, provi ded that such persons have not commit ted any atrocious crime during their being members of such party. Article 2. þÿ The persons alluded to in the present Decree, who submit thereto, will remain under such restrictions as the Executive Power will deem it neces sary to impose on them, and in accordance with the extent of their culpability Article 3. þÿ All individuals who were implicated, accused, or under arrest, as prisoners, can lay claim to this amnesty, within 8 days of its publication in the place where they are detained, either personally, or through the medium of the person who will respectively represent their case before the Judge, who will cause the applicatiou to be recorded in due form, and giving notice of the same to the Executive Power, with a statement of the names, age, circumstances and rank of the delinquent : if worthy

of pardon, according to the result of the examination of the case, or for the banishment or confiscation which it would be necessary to impose on htm. Article 4. þÿ To those persons who, in some manner, were implicated in said commotion, and although not under prosecution, the term of one month is noti lied to them, if they are in the territory of the Republic, to avail themselves of this Amnesty. To those who may be absent from the country, two months notice is given, from the period of the publication of this Decree. Article 5. þÿ The individuals referred to, in the foregoing Article, must pre sent themselves before the Governor of the Province, wherein they may be found, who will, immediately, make bis report to the Executive Power, that through the Secretary of the luterior, the application for amnesty may be made. Article 6. þÿ Those who do not desire to accept the amnesty, which is conceded to them, by this Decree, will remain sub ject to the ordinary course of the laws, and amenable to the penalty determined by it in similar cases. Article 7. þÿ The Executive Power reserves to itself to reduce or extend the term of expulsion or confinement, alter the expulsion or confinement, and change its locality, if it deems it convenient. Article 8. þÿ The parties amnestied or prolonged, lose their rank, employment, titles, privileges and pensions. Article 9. þÿ The Secretary of State o! the Department of the Interior, Justice, and Foreign Relations, remain charged with the execution of this Decree, to be

reported to congress at its next session- Signed, &.c., &.c., Caracas, 23rd August, 1853. JOSE GIIEGORIO MONAGAS. For the President of the Republic þÿ the Secretary of State, Department ot the Interior, Justice, and Foreign Rela t ions. (Signed) SIMON PLANA, S.

A most disgraceful and brutal occurrence took place here this morning, which I shall take the liberty of communicating to you, thinking it probable that no other person here may take the trouble. Being an eye-witness, I have given nothing but what you may rely upon as facts. About seven o'clock this morning an attempt was made by a person calling himself " Deputy Marshal Wynkoop" (a brother to Colonel Wynkoop), another, answering to the name of Joe " Jenkins," and three other assistants from Virginia, to arrest, as a fugitive slave, a coloured waiter in the dining-room of the Phflcnix Hotel in this place. Immediately after receiving their breakfasts at the hands of" Bill," the unsuspecting fugitive, who is a tall, noble-looking, j ed remarkably intelligent, and active mulatto, nearly white, they suddenly from behind knocked liirn down with a mace, and partially shackled him ; but, by a desperate effort, and after a most severe struggle, with the whole five upon him, lie shook them off, and, with the aid of | his handcufs, which were only fast upon

wounds on the countenances of some of the Southerners, the marks of which they will probably carry to their graves. But, notwithstanding the fearful odds against him, he managed to break from their grasp, and, with the loss of everything upon him but a part of his shirt, and covered with blood, he rushed from the house and plunged in the river close by, exclaiming, " I will be drowned, rather than taken alive." His pursuers fired twice at liiin on his way to the river

He replied, "I will die first." They then deliberately fired at him four or five different times, the last ball supposed to have struck on his head, for his face was instantly covered with blood, and the poor fellow sprang and shrieked out in agony, and no doubt would have sunk but for the buoyancy of the water holding him up. From the. Observer, September 25, 1853. TURK E V. CONSTANTINOPLE, Sept. 18. The excitement which prevails among all classes of the Turkish population in Constantinople, and the great placards public Vendues in accordance with posted up in various parts are of the most irritating and incendiary kind, tending to rouse the fiercest passions of the populace. Several persons, on whom suspicion lighted as the authors of these dangerous documents, were arrested, but, for want of sufficient proof to trace the fact home to them, were subsequent ly liberated. Two classes of persons in particular are mentioned from whom these productions are believed to emanate þÿ namely, the religious fanatics and

the scriveners. Those of the former are remarkable no less for their gross ignorance than for their extreme violence ; those of the latter for the insidious manner in which they are drawn up, which does not prevent them from being quite as dangerous, notwithstanding the skill which would conceal the venom of their charges against the Russian section ot the Turkish Cabinet. In both the Ministers are accused ol cowardice or ot treachery, and the allies of the Porte, but particularly England anil France, are held up to the reprobation of the nation. Both demand þÿ war to the þÿdeath þÿ the former undisguisedly, the second more covertly þÿ and war even without the cooperation or assent of the allies. Rescind Pasha is reported to have declared that if Russia will not accept the note modified by the Porte and by the four Ambassadors at Constantinople, war will surely be the consequence. The opinion is that, if war breaks out, hostilities will first take place in Amatolia, Batoun, near the Caucasus. The Egyptian troops, to the number of 14,347, left in the afternoon of the 5th for Varna, on board 1 1 war steamers. They are mostly old soldiers, accustomed to warfare, superior to the Turks, and, þÿ consequently superior to the þÿRussians.! Lord þÿRedchfie s position was very unpleasant ; he sees very few persons, with the exception of the Minister for Foreign Affairs. The manifesto of the Porte to the nation appeared on the 4th in the official journal of Constantinople. It declares that the

note adopted by the Conference of Vienna was of a nature not to be accepted by the Porte, inasmuch as its concession was not compatible with the þÿSultan s ures, and the desire not to be deprived dignity and the independence of his Empire. The placards found on the walls of Constantinople held out a plain threat of rebellion should the Sultan accede to an ignominious peace, conceding any advantages to the Russians. One in the nature of a proclamation wound up by saying, that if Abdul Medjid did not act in a manner worthy of the Ottoman nation, another Sultan could he found who would, and that there were ten thousand true believers ready to follow him. Very great importance is not to be attached to this circumstance individually. The tact, however, that the bulk of the Osmaulis eschew the idea of bowing in any way to Russian prepotcnce is significant; and if that feeling was implicitly listened to þÿ if foreign influences had not stepped between þÿ hostilities would long ere this have commenced on the Danube. . The Emperor of Russia has not scrupled to proclaim a crusade, in the name of his Church, against a people whose prominent feature has at all times been fanaticism. The Sultan has raised no standard in the name of the Moslem faith for the cause of the Prophet. The elements for a fanatic war of religion are, however, plentiful in the Turkish empire; and it requires little penetration to be convinced that þÿ Allah and the þÿProphet! is a cry to which thousands respond readily þÿ the magic chain that

3ST 0 4 <®> )£ 5E ATI ts. unites all Moslem hearts. At the review held last Tuesday by the Sultan in person, the Egyptian troops received their monarch with the cry, þÿ Allah, hunt me yansour Soultanena þÿ! (O God, come to the aid of our Sultan !) The Bey of Tunis has informed the Porte that his contingent is ready to take the field. Steamers are about to be sent for these troops to reinforce the garrison of Constantinople. Izzctt Pasha, late Governor of Tripoli, has been appointed to the governorship of Belgrade, with orders to depart at once and assume the functions of his office. The Russian subjects and thaproteges of that nation who have remained at Constantinople have carried on such a propaganda against the Turkish Government, either verbally or by the publication of pamphlets, that Rescind Pasha, the Minister of Foreign Affairs, was compelled to request the Russian Consul-General to warn his countrymen, and to put an end to their hlameable conduct. The following is a copy of one of the placards which have been posted up in Constantinople : þÿ þÿ O most powerful Padishah ! for the love of your august person all your subjects are ready to sacrifice their lives, their property, and their families; but it is your duty to draw from the scabbard the sword of the victorious Mahomet, which you put on in the mosque of Ayouh Ansari, in imitation of your illustrious ancestors and predecessors. Your ministers display hesitation, because they are dominated by the passion for pleas-

of them. A great danger menaces us. In such a state of things may God preserve us all! Your victorious army and all the nation demand absolutely to combat for your incontestable rights. O Padishah! open your cars and listen to the voice of your þÿchildren! Ayouh Ansari, mentioned above, is an illustrious personage of Mussulman history, a contemporary of Mahomet, who powerfully aided him in the propagation of Islamism, and was killed in the first expedition of the Mussulmans against the Greek empire.

Head-quarters of the Turkish Army (Varna), Sept. þÿ þÿ 2. The greatest activity reigns here, both as regards the preparation of defensive measures and the instruction of the troops. þÿ þÿ Omer Pasha is well worthy of the renown attached to his name. lie takes advantage of every eventuality and circumstance, and has made the most judicious dispositions. The army, which now numbers 100,000 men, 10 regiments of cavalry, and 250 pieces of artillery, is disposed in brigades of 10,000 men each, provided with artillery and cavalry, and stationed all along the banks of the Danube, and in many lines towards the interior ; so that on whatever point the enemy should present himself, after having forced the passage of the river, which is guarded by batteries and fortifications, he would have to engage with a Turkish force as strong as himself, which would be rapidly concentrated to meet him. This is the main drift of the defensive operations of the Cornmanderin-Chicf. þÿ Uriel.

Fatness a Beauty. þÿ The women of Egypt, in order to acquire a degree of fatness bathe themselves several days in lukewarm water. They stay so long in their baths, that they eat and drink therein. During the time they are in the bath they take every half-hour some broth made of a fat pullet, and stuffed with sweet almonds, hazel nuts, dales, and pistachio nuts. After taking this sort of broth four times, they eat a fat pullet all but the head. When they come out of the bath, they are rubbed over with perfumes and sweet-scented pomatum, and after that some of them take myrobalans before going to bed ; others take a draught prepared with gum tragacanth and sugar-candy.

Origin of Texts. þÿ The taking of a text seems to have originated with Ezra, who, accompanied by several Levites, in a public congregation of men and women, ascended a pulpit, opened tha book of the law, and after addressing a prayer to the Deity, to which the people said Amen, þÿ read in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the þÿreading. Previously to that time the Patriarchs delivered in public assemblies either prophecies or ! moral instructions for the edification of the people. It was not until after the return of the Jews from Babylonish captivity, during which period they had almost lost the language in which the j Tuff? And the thing the Pentateuch was written, that it became necessary to explain as well as to read Scripture to them þÿ a practice adopted by Ezra, and since universally followed. In latter times the book of Moses was thus read in the synagogue every Sabbath day. To this custom the Saviour conformed, and in a synagogue .at Nazareth read passages from the Prophet Isaiah; then closing the book returned it to the priest, and preached from the text. This custom, which now prevails ;
rupted in the dark ages, when the ethics of Aristotle were read in many churches on Sunday, instead of the Holy Scriptures.

The sudden depression j of those with whom they are connected, would give Felicity ; but iftliey are exalted in the scale of society, and receive the just encomiums of merit, it creates hatred. They now cease to be upon a level with such ; and as they will not see by what principles they have been distanced, they seek to avoid comparison, and be- <lin to detract either from the moral or intellectual qualities of those whom they once loved. Thus merit is frequently immolated upon the altar of caprice, or devoted to the sullen look of suspicion.

The Sabbath. þÿ The rest of the Sabbath is as necessary after the engagement of the Week, as is the þÿnight rest s after the work of the day. To the one we go instinctively, forced by fatigue. It is well if we observe the other ; impelled by mortal consideration, before suffering the penalty attached to its violation, of which no instinct gives us warning. After six days of labor our strained muscles need a season to renew their elasticity þÿ our irritable nerves to recover their normal state þÿ our fretted spirits to resume their equanimity. A simple change of necessary labour does a great deal ; the entire cessation ol all that is necessary does still more. The fitting devotional exercises of the day are calming and soothing, and productive of that healthy state of mind with which it is desirable to enter upon the honest duties of the succeeding day. The influence of the Sabbath on the þÿweek tumultuous s cares, is like oil poured on a stormy sea. Stretched out over the hurrying crowd of daily engagements like the rod of the Prophet over the Red Sea, it piles the waves up on either side, and we pass through them dryshod.

The signal made at the Telegraph at 3 þÿo clock on Thursday afternoon last for the Royal Mail þÿCompany s crew-propeller Esk, Captain Taylor, announced to our Inhabitants the approach of Ilis Excellency Governor H. I). F. FED- DERSEN, K. i)., who it was previously known would take passage in the abovenamed vessel from Saint Croix to this Island. As the Esk rounded the point, His þÿExcellency s Fiag at the Main set a large portion of our community in motion to be in readiness at the þÿKinjr s Wharf to receive the Governor at his landing. The Esk, we are told, left Christiansted at meridian on Thursday, and her passage might on this occasion be called an extraordinary one, were we not reminded of the strong breezes we enjoyed during that day. On entering t he harbor the Esk shaped her course along the shores of the careening hole, affording those on board an opportunity of getting a full starboard view of the steamer Solent, as she now majestically rides our waters, and then veered round her stern, and steamed up the larboard quarter. This was no doubt done to enable His Excellency to have an interesting sight ot that beautifully-constructed steam-ship. Soon after, the Captain of the Port, Captain T. A. Kjr; and the þÿCommandant s Aide, Captain Hansen, went alongside the Esk þÿ moored to the buoy at the head of the harbour þÿ and His þÿExcellency F s lag was lowered as he stepped into the barge which was prepared to receive him. On His Ex-

þÿcellency s reaching the wharf a salute was fired from Fort Christian, and as he landed the Honorable II. II. Berg, Commandant, Ac., «fcc., attended by Major v. Castonier, Major Wolfe, Major v. Strandga ard, with the Officers attached to their respective Corps, both Military and Militia, the Civil Officers, and a few private Gentlemen, tendered him a most gracious welcome. During the past few days the weather has undergone a very favorable change þÿ the overpowering heat gradually giving place to a cooler atmosphere. Several refreshing showers of rain have also fallen during the week. Our hurricane season has fairly passed over without our having to chronicle any disaster whatever in the harbor or on shore, and the shipping begin to exhibit an animated appearance, from daily arrivals.

A gentleman who arrived yesterday from Tortola informs us that the Legislative Council and Assembly ot the Virgin Islands had met on Thursday last, when was read a Despatch (rom the Secretary of State for the Colonies received by the last packet from England enclosing an Order from the Queen in Council, expressing Her þÿMajesty reso- s lution of adhering to the original intention ot withdrawing the Troops from most of the British Colonies þÿ and recommending that measures be immediately adopted at Tortola for the organisation of an efficient Militia force for the protection of the Colony, which measure would receive the sanction of the Home Government ! We opine that if this be really the fixed determination of the Parent State, Tortola would soon be an abandoned wilderness, as no respectable inhabitant could then be persuaded to remain on the Island ! Already we learn that some of the principal landed proprietors have sold out their estates in Tortola, and are in treaty lor the purchase of others in Saint Croix, where they intend to retire ! þÿ So much for the Duke of Newcastle ! !

RELAXATIONS OF GREAT MEN. Men of the strongest minds need relaxation. The bow can not always be kept bent, otherwise its elasticity is irretrievably injured. Like it, the human mind must be relaxed from time to time, to allow it to recover its strength and

tone. This lesson is well taught in the , traditionary story related of the Apostle John. A hunter one day passing, appeared much surprised at seeing him caressing a little bird with all the delight of a child. The well-beloved disciple observing his astonishment, said to the hunter, þÿ Why do not you keep your bow always bent þÿV þÿ Because it would soon lose its strength if it were always þÿstrung. þÿ Well! replied the old man, þÿ would it be the same with my mind ; if I gave it no relaxation, it would, in like manner, lose its þÿforce. It is interesting to note the amusements of learned and great men of present and past times. Their predilections, their private tastes, their amusements, their domestic habits, their relaxations þÿ in a word, all that satisfies them, annoys them, amuses them þÿ are capable of furnishing useful lessons to our race ; for a þÿman m s anners and habits help us to a knowledge of him, and are the best evidence of his real character. Many great men have delighted in passing their hours of relaxation in the company of children. This betokens a pure and loving nature. Richter says, the man is to he shunned who does not love the society of children. Henry IV. was passionately fond of them, and delighted in their gambols and little caprices. One day, when crawling round his room on all-fours, on his hands and knees, with the Dauphin on his back, and the other children about him urging the king to gallop in imitation of a horse, an embassador suddenly entered and

surprised the royal family in the midst of their fun. Henry, without rising to his feet, asked, þÿ Have you children, Mr, þÿEmbassador? þÿ Yes þÿsire. þÿ In that case I proceed with the þÿsport, replied the king. The Duke of Wellington was, in like manner, extremely fond of children, and was a general favorite with them. He enjoyed their gambols, took part in them, and was constantly presenting them with little keepsakes and presents. The opera was his chief amusement; and he was a regular frequenter of both houses as well as of the Ancient and other first class concerts. Leibnitz used to pass months together in his. study, engaged with his laborious investigations. At such times his only relaxation consisted in collecting about him in his study children of both sexes, whom he watched; and sometimes he took part in their frolics. Seated in his easy chair, he delighted to observe their lively movements, to listen to their conversation, and to observe their several dispositions; and when his soul had sufficiently enjoyed the innocent spectacle, he would dismiss the children with sweetmeats, and return to his studies with renewed energy. þÿ Harper's Magazine.

Fluency of Speech. þÿ The common fluency of speech in many men, and most women, is owing to a scarcity of matter and a scarcity of words ; for whoever is master of a language, and has a mind full of ideas, will be apt, in speaking to hesitate upon the choice of both ; whereas, common speakers have only one set of ideas, and one set of words to clothe them ; and these are always ready at the mouth ; so people can come faster out of church when it is almost empty, than when a crowd is at the þÿAoor.
